findings.paper_title: 20261015 Agenda Item 18 -Appendix A -Investment Strategy Statement - docx
findings.headline: Fund participating in Border to Coast pooled arrangement with mediation framework for situations where Pool cannot implement Fund's full investment strategy
findings.detail: Fund invests through Border to Coast Pensions Partnership (FCA-regulated), owned equally by all participating authorities. All investment management decisions supporting strategy implementation must be made by Pool. Fund recognises full alignment between local strategy and pooled arrangement may not always be possible. Where this occurs, mediation routes available include Pool explaining non-implementable elements, supporting Fund to understand how strategy could be adjusted to be deliverable, and collective engagement to increase scalability of chosen strategy.
findings.matters: Shows governance structure for managing tension between individual fund preferences and pooling efficiency; peers will face similar pooling governance challenges and mediation requirements
findings.figures: Border to Coast FRN 800511 (FCA registration)
findings.quote: The Pool must take all reasonable steps to implement the investment strategy set by the Fund. The Fund recognises that full alignment by the Pool may not always be possible and might run counter to the fundamental aims of pooling. Should this situation occur, the following mediation routes are available

findings.paper_title: 20261015 Agenda Item 18 -Appendix A -Investment Strategy Statement - docx
findings.headline: Fund established 0-5% local investment target but implementation awaiting formation of Bedfordshire local strategic authority
findings.detail: The Committee has set a target range of 0-5% for local investment in the portfolio, defined as Bedfordshire and neighbouring counties. Local investment is not a separate allocation but will represent a portion of main asset classes such as Real Estate and Private Equity. Implementation cannot proceed until the relevant strategic authority is formed in Bedfordshire. The Committee must first resolve questions on return targets, local priorities suitable for pension fund investment, and impact measurement arrangements.
findings.matters: Demonstrates how pension fund strategy implementation is dependent on external local government reorganization outcomes; other councils in areas facing devolution or restructuring will be watching how Bedford manages this dependency
findings.figures: 0-5% local investment target range
findings.quote: Further work is required to implement this allocation over the life of this ISS (and longer). In particular, the Committee and Fund Officers will work with the relevant strategic authority - once one has been formed in Bedfordshire - to identify the types of investment likely to both generate the returns required by the Fund together with impacts which will positively assist the delivery of local growth plans.

findings.paper_title: 20261015 Agenda Item 18 -Appendix A -Investment Strategy Statement - docx
findings.headline: Fund investment strategy targets 8.3% annual returns and 100% funding level over 20 years with greater than 75% success probability
findings.detail: Based on July 2026 modelling, the fund's best estimate expected return on assets is 8.3% per annum over 20 years at the 50th percentile. Liability modelling from December 2025 established the current strategy should deliver a 100% funding level over 20 years with likelihood of success greater than 75%. Expected one-year volatility of returns is 12.6%.
findings.matters: Shows fund's expected ability to meet pension liabilities without requiring escalating employer contributions; peers and lenders would benchmark their own fund return targets and funding prospects against comparable targets
findings.figures: 8.3% p.a. expected return; 100% funding target; >75% success probability; 12.6% expected one-year volatility
findings.quote: Based on modelling undertaken in July 2026 the best estimate expected return on the Fund's assets was 8.3% p.a. over 20-years (50 percentile median returns). Through the recent liability modelling exercise in December 2025, we have established the current strategy should deliver a funding level of 100% over 20 years with a likelihood of success of greater than 75% over a 20 year time horizon.

findings.headline: LGPS (Pooling, Management and Investment of Funds) Regulations 2026 came into force 30 June 2026, legally requiring all investments under pool management

findings.paper_title: Item 11 Annual Treasury Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Fair value losses of £1.65 million on pooled fund investments; statutory accounting protection expires 31 March 2029
findings.detail: The council holds £33.35 million in pooled fund investments carrying unrealised mark-to-market losses of £1.65 million at 31 March 2026, down from £2.66m the prior year but still material. These losses are currently protected from the general fund by Statutory Instrument 2018 No. 1207. However, this override expires on 31 March 2029, after which fair value movements will impact the council's revenue account. The council has begun making provisions in its Medium Term Financial Strategy to manage this impact.
findings.matters: In three years, material mark-to-market losses will flow through the revenue account, affecting the council's general fund and reserves; lenders and finance directors need to understand this emerging exposure and whether provisions will be adequate.

findings.detail: The statutory override allows accumulated DSG deficits to be carried forward without charging to the General Fund, providing temporary relief. The DfE is funding 90% of the deficit accumulated up to 31 March 2026 via the High Needs Stability Grant. The council has submitted a DSG Deficit Recovery Plan to the DfE as part of national SEND reform, acknowledging that meaningful improvement will take medium to long term and will be driven by expanding local provision, strengthening mainstream inclusion and improving commissioning.
findings.matters: The override expiry creates a contingent liability risk if (a) the 90% funding assumption is not confirmed or (b) the deficit continues to grow. This is an identified medium-term financial risk with no current mitigation plan in place within the MTFS.
findings.figures: Override expires 31 March 2028. Assumption: DfE funds 90% of accumulated deficit from 2028/29 onwards.
findings.quote: There is currently a statutory override in place that allows authorities to carry forward a deficit on the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG), that is not charged to the General Fund. The statutory override is due to expire at the end of 2027/2028.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 MTFS covering report
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation forecast to increase by an average of 5 households per month over the MTFS period as baseline trend
findings.detail: The council faces a national trend of rising temporary accommodation use, compounded by upcoming legislation (Renters Reform Bill, Social Housing Regulation). However, the council's budget monitoring and savings reports position actual numbers below the national average trend increase, expecting delivery of transformation actions (Transformation Housing Action Plan and Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy 2024–2029) to moderate growth. The focus is on prevention, increasing supply of settled accommodation, and digital tools for rent monitoring.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is volatile and demand-driven, creating unpredictable cost exposure. While the forecast is prudent, legislative changes and housing market conditions present downside risk if prevention targets are not met.
findings.figures: Forecast growth: 5 households per month average (2027/28–2030/31)
findings.quote: The medium-term modelling therefore, factors in an average increase of circa 5 households per month, based on a 12-month rolling average, with cost increases in line with CPI inflation as a baseline rising trend.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 MTFS covering report
findings.headline: Adults services forecast 4% annual demand growth and care package inflation of 3.7%, driven by complexity of need and transitions from children's services
findings.detail: Demand growth is underpinned by increased numbers of young people with learning disabilities transitioning to adult care, adults with neurodivergent needs, and rising mental health support needs. Inflation on care packages is calculated as a blended rate: 70% of the living wage increase estimate and 30% CPI. Department of Health has announced a new Negotiating Body to determine pay and terms for care workers from 2028/29 with £500m provided nationally for first year, but no additional cost has been included in the MTFS to date.
findings.matters: Adult social care is a statutory service with demand-driven cost exposure. The dual pressure of volume growth plus inflation creates compounding cost increases difficult to absorb through efficiency alone. The pending fair pay agreement for care workers creates additional unquantified cost risk from 2028/29.
findings.figures: Demand growth: 4% annual. Care package inflation: 3.7% (2027/28–2028/29), 3.5% (2029/30–2030/31).
findings.quote: The forecasts assume a growth in care packages demand of 4% across the board. Care package inflation is established through a blended rate (70% upper element of low pay commission estimate of living wage increase and 30% CPI).

findings.paper_title: Item 13 MTFS covering report
findings.headline: Children's services forecast includes £6.727 million catch-up cost from 2026/27 and residential placement inflation of 15% in 2027/28
findings.detail: The council faces both a delayed cost impact from the current year (catch-up) and market-driven inflation on placements. Residential placement inflation is described as reflecting national trend of 15–22.5% owing to shortage of foster carers, driving demand for residential care where choices are scarce and private providers can set high prices. The council has a statutory duty to place children where assessed as in need. From 2027/28, the forecast assumes negative growth (fewer placements) in line with service plans to reduce high-cost residential placements and looked-after children numbers.
findings.matters: Children's social care cost growth is outpacing inflation and is noted across all councils. The market concentration in private providers creates price risk outside the council's control. The Association of Directors of Children's Services is lobbying government for systemic intervention (market rebalancing, shift to not-for-profit models) because the system is described as 'broken and unsustainable'.
findings.figures: Catch-up cost 2027/28: £6.727m. Residential placement inflation 2027/28: 15%; 2028/29–2030/31: 5% each year.
findings.quote: The 2027/28 forecast includes a 'catch-up' element to reflect the forecast pressure from the current financial year of £6.727 million... Inflation on residential placements has been included in line with the national trend which is currently between 15% to 22.5%.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 MTFS covering report
findings.headline: General Fund balance rebuilt to £14.2 million at 31 March 2026 from £9.6 million prior year, but positioned at lower end of revised risk-assessed range of £14.6 million to £17.8 million
findings.detail: The council has made progress rebuilding reserves after prior depletion but acknowledges the current position sits below the prudent minimum level. The MTFS includes assumptions to re-establish the General Fund at the mid-range point (approximately £16.2m) by 31 March 2028. The risk assessment has been updated to align with risk register levels and better reflect exposure to demographic and inflationary risks.
findings.matters: Reserves below the risk-assessed minimum reduce financial resilience and ability to absorb unexpected pressures. The council's plan to rebuild takes two years, meaning exposure remains elevated in the near term.
findings.figures: GF balance 31 March 2026: £14.2m (prior year £9.6m). Risk-assessed range: £14.6m–£17.8m. Target: mid-point ~£16.2m by 31 March 2028.
findings.quote: As at the 31 March 2026, the General Fund balance stood at £14.2 million; this is an increase from the balance of £9.6 million as at 31 March 2025... the range of financial risk was revised as part of the outturn process as being in range of £14.6 million and £17.8 million.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 MTFS covering report
findings.headline: Best Value Inspection announced 31 March 2026 under Part 1 of the Local Government Act 1999; report to be published in autumn
findings.detail: This is a formal intervention mechanism requiring the council to make arrangements to secure continuous improvement in economy, efficiency and effectiveness. The council has established an Independent Improvement and Assurance Panel composed of external experts to provide guidance, challenge and scrutiny of its Improvement Plan and progress on budget deficits. The Panel reports directly to MHCLG.
findings.matters: A Best Value Inspection signals formal concern about council performance. The presence of external assurance panels indicates central government oversight of financial recovery plans. Such interventions often precede further escalation if improvement is not demonstrated.
findings.figures: Inspection announced 31 March 2026; report expected autumn 2026
findings.quote: On 31 March 2026, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) announced a Best Value Inspection under Part 1 of the Local Government Act 1999 which requires councils to make arrangements to secure continuous improvement in the way their functions are exercised, having regard to a combination of economy, efficiency and effectiveness.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 MTFS covering report
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 settlement left Bedford with 4.8% increase in Core Spending Power for 2026/27, below national average of 5.7% and below its deprivation group average of 5.9%
findings.detail: Comparative analysis shows Bedford would have received approximately £4.5m additional annual funding by 2028/29 if its increase matched the all-England average. Regionally, the shortfall against West Midlands, East Midlands and Yorkshire & Humber authorities is estimated at £14.0m, £11.4m and £11.4m respectively on a cumulative basis. The council was disadvantaged despite the FFR 2.0's stated intention to rebalance funding toward more deprived authorities.
findings.matters: The council's funding trajectory is weaker than peer authorities facing similar pressures, materially narrowing fiscal headroom. This adversely affects ability to absorb further demand pressures without supplementary support.
findings.figures: Bedford CSP increase 4.8% vs national average 5.7% (2026/27); cumulative 13.2% vs 15.3% across spending review period. Shortfall: ~£4.5m per annum by 2028/29 vs all-England; £14.0m vs West Midlands, £11.4m vs East Midlands/Yorkshire.
findings.quote: The average increase in CSP for 2026/27 for all England authorities equated to 5.7%, compared to a 4.8% increase for Bedford Borough Council.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 MTFS covering report
findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap of £38.9 million forecast over 2027/28 to 2030/31, with £29.1 million in opening year
findings.detail: The central case forecast shows a sharp front-loaded gap: £29.1m in 2027/28, reducing to £5.6m in 2028/29, then £1.1m and £3.1m. Identified savings total £16.4m over the period, heavily weighted to 2027/28 (£10.5m), leaving a shortfall to be bridged. The council notes that a full savings programme will be reported 18 November 2026.
findings.matters: The gap is substantial relative to the council's budget envelope and savings plans so far identified cover only 42% of the cumulative gap. Early delivery of savings proposals is critical to avoid further need for exceptional support or service reductions.
findings.quote: The cumulative gap for the period 2027/28 to 2030/31 of £38.9 million represents a significant proportion of the Council's current net budget.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 MTFS covering report
findings.headline: Council required £25 million Exceptional Financial Support to set 2026/27 budget; without it, section 114 notice would have been issued
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget, approved 18 February 2026, is the first sign of the scale of pressure facing the council. EFS was provided alongside 36 other councils. The council is currently within budget envelope for 2026/27 (August monitoring), though this requires tight financial control to maintain through year end.
findings.matters: A council on the verge of section 114 insolvency is a material credit event and indicator of structural budget stress. The need for emergency funding signals inability to balance through ordinary means.
findings.figures: £25 million Exceptional Financial Support provided alongside 36 other councils for 2026/27
findings.quote: The 2026/27 Budget approved on 18 February 2026 is supported by £25 million Exceptional Financial Support (alongside 36 other councils) without which it would be necessary to issue a s114 notice.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Appendix A CP Dashboard - 2026-27 - Q1
findings.headline: Customer services call handling underperforming: 71.2% of calls answered against 80% target
findings.detail: Q1 performance declined to 71.2% call answer rate (down from 72.4% in Q4 2025/26) against a target of 80%. Council attributes pressure to sustained high demand across multiple service areas, including campaigns for environmental services food caddy and council tax. Response includes recruitment to vacant posts and upskilling of new advisors.
findings.matters: Persistent gap between demand and capacity signals resource constraint that may require investment; sustained underperformance against target flags service delivery risk
findings.figures: 71.2% answered in Q1 2026/27 vs 72.4% in Q4 2025/26; target 80%
findings.quote: Performance during Q1 was below the desired level and highlights the continued pressure on the service from increased demand. Call volumes have remained high across a number of service areas, impacting our ability to answer all calls presented.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Appendix A CP Dashboard - 2026-27 - Q1
findings.headline: Adult social care assessment backlog clearing: 50.5% of assessments completed within 28-day target, up from 48.2% year-on-year
findings.detail: Q1 2026/27 delivered 50.5% of assessments within 28 days (78 of 92 cases), compared to 48.2% in Q1 2025/26 (186 of 386 cases). Council delivered 47 additional assessments within target timescale. Improvement driven by triage of referrals based on risk and need, THRIVE front-door model implementation, and Adult Services Improvement Plan actions.
findings.matters: Clearing backlog reduces delayed cost attribution, improves service flow, and signals emerging capacity to handle future demand without additional pressure
findings.figures: 50.5% (78 of 92) in Q1 2026/27 vs 48.2% (186 of 386) in Q1 2025/26; 47 additional assessments completed within target
findings.quote: This represents an overall increase of 75 assessments and 47 more assessments within 28 days. Improvement work includes ongoing triage of referrals based on risk and need, implementation of the THRIVE front-door model, and delivery of actions within the Adult Services Improvement Plan.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Appendix A CP Dashboard - 2026-27 - Q1
findings.headline: Residential children's home placements increasing, shifting costs from lower-cost foster care
findings.detail: Council identifies increased reliance on residential children's homes as contributing to placement instability and more frequent moves for children in care. In response, council is rolling out a third Mockingbird constellation to stabilise foster placements. Mockingbird groups provide support to foster families through small connected networks.
findings.matters: Shift from foster care (lower cost) to residential placement (higher cost per child) creates direct budget pressure in children's services; finance directors need to understand the cost trajectory
findings.figures: Not quantified in paper
findings.quote: The increased use of residential children's homes contributes to the increased number of moves with our children in care. We are working to identify children at risk of placement breakdown to reduce this pressure and support children to remain where they are.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Appendix A CP Dashboard - 2026-27 - Q1
findings.headline: Section 42 safeguarding enquiries increased 94% year-on-year to 97 open cases by end June 2026
findings.detail: Open safeguarding enquiries rose from 50 in June 2025 to 97 by end June 2026, with a 20% increase between May and June alone. Council notes safeguarding pressures have intensified and requires sustained management oversight. Mitigations include prioritising high-risk enquiries and maintaining strong management oversight to progress investigations in a timely way.
findings.matters: Escalating safeguarding demand signals urgent operational and cost pressure requiring resource investment; other councils and lenders need to understand if this is a localised spike or part of a broader trend
findings.figures: 97 open enquiries vs 50 in June 2025; 20% increase from May to June 2026; 94% increase year-on-year
findings.quote: Safeguarding pressures have increased. There were 97 open Section 42 enquiries at the end of June, compared with 81 in May and 50 in June 2025. This represents a 20% increase since May and a 94% increase compared with last year.

findings.paper_title: Item 12 Treasury Mgmt Performance Mid Year Review 2026-27
findings.headline: Interest receivable forecast to outachieve budget by £0.350m due to higher balances and delayed rate cuts.
findings.detail: Interest receivable is forecast to outachieve budget by £0.350m. This reflects higher cash balances than forecast being held in Money Market Funds for longer durations, combined with the Bank of England maintaining base rate at 3.75% rather than cutting as anticipated when the budget was set. MMF yields are between 3.75% and 3.85%.
findings.matters: A positive variance but one dependent on external factors and delayed capital receipts, which may not persist if rate cuts materialise or income flows normalise.
findings.figures: Interest Receivable: budget £1.885m, forecast £2.235m (outachievement £0.350m). Base rate 3.75%, MMF yields 3.75-3.85%.
findings.quote: The forecast is for the budget to be overachieved due to higher balances than forecast allowing the Council to hold more funds in Money Market Funds for longer durations, with the Bank of England not cutting rates as forecast when the budget was calculated.

findings.paper_title: Item 12 Treasury Mgmt Performance Mid Year Review 2026-27
findings.headline: Council took £10m PWLB borrowing at 5 and 10 year durations to rebalance maturity structure within prudential limits.
findings.detail: During the first half of 2026/27, the council borrowed £10m from PWLB split across 5 and 10 year tenors (average duration 7.5 years) to bring the maturity structure back within prudential indicator levels. Despite unfavourable rate conditions, further long-term borrowing is likely to be required before year-end to manage refinancing risk as the 0-3 years bucket is at the 65% upper limit.
findings.matters: Demonstrates active refinancing management prioritising duration risk over interest rate risk, and signals expectation of further borrowing despite adverse conditions.
findings.figures: £10m new PWLB borrowing, 7.5 years average duration. Maturity structure: 0-3 years 65% (upper limit), 3-10 years 19%, over 10 years 15%.
findings.quote: During the first half of the current year the Council has taken out loans with the PWLB totalling £10 million for an average duration of 7.5 years across two loans. This has brought the structure of borrowing back within the indicator levels.

findings.paper_title: Item 12 Treasury Mgmt Performance Mid Year Review 2026-27
findings.headline: Investment fair value losses will impact revenue from 2029/30 when statutory instrument expires, reducing spending capacity.
findings.detail: The council currently holds £0.709m in unrealised fair value losses on pooled fund investments. These are not charged to revenue under Statutory Instrument 2018 No. 1207, which expires 31 March 2029. From 2029/30 onwards, all fair value movements will impact the revenue account and General Fund. The Medium-Term Financial Strategy allows for this impact, but it represents a known permanent reduction in available resources.
findings.matters: This is a quantified future revenue pressure that will permanently reduce the council's spending capacity in three years' time unless offset by savings or income growth.
findings.figures: Current pooled funds: £31m principal, £30.291m NAV (fair value loss £0.709m). Statutory Instrument 2018 No. 1207 expires 31 March 2029. Fundamentum REIT exception would generate £0.051m gain.
findings.quote: Statutory Instrument 2018 No. 1207 will expire on 31 March 2029. This will mean fair value movements from 2029/30 will impact the Council's revenue account and General Fund.

findings.paper_title: Item 12 Treasury Mgmt Performance Mid Year Review 2026-27
findings.headline: Investment portfolio returned 5.56% annualised in first third of year against 5.82% target, with property fund weakness.
findings.detail: The council achieved gross return of £0.774m (5.56% annualised) against a target of 5.82%. Underperformance is attributed to pooled fund holdings performing slightly below forecast, particularly the CCLA property fund which fell in value by £0.125m due to interest rate expectations not materialising. The £4m Aegon Diversified fund redemption (at a £0.224m gain) removed 6% interest yield from the portfolio.
findings.matters: Investment income supports service delivery and off-sets borrowing costs. Underperformance of revenue-generating assets requires strategy review.
findings.figures: Gross return £0.774m (5.56% annualised) against 5.82% target. CCLA: £10m principal, £9.514m NAV. Fundamentum REIT: £2m principal, £1.240m NAV.
findings.quote: The rate of return is below forecast target as a result of pooled fund holdings performance being slightly under forecast, especially with the CCLA.

findings.paper_title: Item 12 Treasury Mgmt Performance Mid Year Review 2026-27
findings.headline: Capital spending in 2025/26 lower than anticipated, creating uncertainty in borrowing forecasts and requiring programme review.
findings.detail: Interest payable is forecast to underspend by £1.3m, explained by less short-term borrowing in the first half of 2026/27 than forecast due to capital spend being lower than anticipated during 2025/26. Capital receipts also fell short of forecast. The Capital Programme will be reviewed during the year to allow forecasts to be revised.
findings.matters: Programme slippage directly affects borrowing requirements, debt servicing costs, and the delivery of capital-dependent service improvements.
findings.figures: Interest Payable: forecast £6.597m against budget £7.897m (underspend £1.3m). Total capital financing costs forecast £9.420m against budget £11.070m.
findings.quote: The forecast expenditure is under budget due to less short-term borrowing during the first half of the year than forecast. This is due to capital spend being lower than anticipated during 2025/26. The Capital Programme will be reviewed further during the year, allowing the forecast to be revised.

findings.paper_title: Item 12 Treasury Mgmt Performance Mid Year Review 2026-27
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing of £43m expected to remain due to capital income below budget profile.
findings.detail: The council held £43.0m of short-term borrowing (1-3 months duration) as of 31 July 2026, which is expected to persist as income is currently below the budgeted profile. Greater income is expected in the second half of the year from capital receipts, CIL, s106 and DSG High Needs Grant. This creates a structural refinancing requirement and places 0-3 years borrowing at the 65% upper prudential limit.
findings.matters: Persistent short-term borrowing at this scale creates refinancing and interest rate risk, and indicates capital income forecasting is materially off-track.
findings.figures: £43.0m short-term borrowing held 31 July 2026 at 1-3 months. Maturity profile: 0-3 years at 65% (upper limit). 0.3 year borrowing actual £48m (48% of total).
findings.quote: Short-term borrowing is expected to remain at current levels for the remainder of 2026/27 as income is currently below the budgeted profile, and therefore greater income is expected in the second half of the year, especially around capital receipts, CIL, s106 and DSG High Needs Grant.

findings.paper_title: Item 12 Treasury Mgmt Performance Mid Year Review 2026-27
findings.headline: External borrowing forecast to rise from £102.5m to £199.9m by March 2028, establishing council as long-term borrower.
findings.detail: The liability benchmark forecasts external borrowing rising substantially from £102.5m at March 2026 to £174.6m at March 2027 and £199.9m at March 2028. This structural shift signals the council will transition from a position of surplus cash to becoming a structural borrower. The borrowing requirement is driven by capital plans and reduced usable reserves falling from £85.6m to £64.2m by 2030.
findings.matters: A near-doubling of external debt over three years transforms the council's financial position and creates sustained exposure to interest rate risk and refinancing requirements.
findings.figures: External borrowing: £102.5m (31.3.26), £174.6m forecast (31.3.27), £199.9m forecast (31.3.28). CFR rising from £203.5m to £280.5m.
findings.quote: The liability benchmark is an important tool to help establish whether the Council is likely to be a long-term borrower or long-term investor in the future, and so shape its strategic focus and decision-making.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 Appendix A MTFS
findings.headline: Council forecasts medium-term budget gap requiring efficiency savings but does not disclose specific deficit figures in this strategy document
findings.detail: The MTFS identifies a funding challenge across 2027-2031, stating that 'resources are not going to be able to sustain the current level of spend' and that 'for the most part this results in a budget gap to be addressed'. The council has implemented a program of service and efficiency reviews to close the gap, but the magnitude of the deficit is not quantified here.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council has identified and quantified its deficit and has developed a credible plan to close it; absence of specific figures in the MTFS raises questions about the precision and credibility of the financial plan
findings.figures: No specific budget gap figures provided
findings.quote: The MTFS sets out the financial challenge across the medium term based on the estimates and known changes in the Council's resources and operations. For the most part this results in a budget gap to be addressed.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 Appendix A MTFS
findings.headline: Universal theme park development will significantly impact infrastructure and service demand, but financial implications remain under assessment
findings.detail: Universal Destinations & Experiences is developing a major theme park and resort in Bedford Borough with works started in 2026 and opening planned for 2031. The council acknowledges the development will have 'significant direct and indirect impact on the authority's infrastructure, service delivery requirements and resources streams' but states it 'will establish processes to understand the associated implications arising from the development', indicating the financial impact to the council has not yet been fully assessed.
findings.matters: A major development of this scale will drive demand for council services (roads, waste, social services, utilities) and could affect business rates income, but uncertainty about net financial impact to the council represents risk
findings.figures: £50 billion estimated economic benefit; 20,000 construction jobs; 8,000 permanent jobs when operational; 8.5 million annual visitors rising to 12.5 million; opening 2031
findings.quote: This development will have a significant direct and indirect impact on the authority's infrastructure, service delivery requirements and resources streams. The authority will establish processes to understand the associated implications arising from the development.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 Appendix A MTFS
findings.headline: External CIPFA Resilience Review found council's financial outlook demanded emergency measures
findings.detail: The council commissioned a CIPFA Resilience Review and received assessment from an Independent Improvement and Assurance Panel. The review determined that 'the financial outlook for Bedford Borough Council demanded emergency measures'. The council has subsequently established new strategic priorities through an Improvement Plan Framework to address financial sustainability.
findings.matters: An independent expert review validates that the council has serious financial problems requiring urgent intervention, providing external verification of the severity of the situation
findings.figures: No figures provided
findings.quote: The report identified that financial outlook for Bedford Borough Council demanded emergency measures and a new set of overarching strategic priorities created to underpin and inform the council's corporate plan.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 Appendix A MTFS
findings.headline: Council's budget strategy is to exit dependency on Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: The council's budget premise is that it 'must move to a financially sustainable position that is not reliant on Exceptional Financial Support as soon as possible'. Exceptional Financial Support is government bailout funding provided to councils in financial distress, indicating the council has previously required rescue funding and remains dependent on it.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council has required government rescue funding previously and whether it is progressing toward financial self-sufficiency
findings.figures: No figures provided
findings.quote: the Council must move to a financially sustainable position that is not reliant on Exceptional Financial Support as soon as possible, whilst recognising demand and inflationary pressures are likely to increase and must be adequately provided for

findings.paper_title: Item 05(ii) References from Budget & Corp OSC 01.10.26
findings.headline: Improvement and transformation activity lacks clearly identified savings
findings.detail: The O&S Committee urged the Executive to ensure transformation expenditure has clearly identified associated savings. The committee's need to urge this suggests transformation spending may currently lack explicit savings linkage.
findings.matters: Capital and revenue transformation spending without articulated savings creates financial risk; lenders assess whether transformation investments yield measurable returns.

findings.detail: The O&S Committee requested the Executive ensure highways funding is fully carried forward rather than lost. This indicates unspent capital allocation that may lapse or be returned.
findings.matters: Unspent capital allocations indicate planning, delivery, or execution problems; lenders assess a council's capability to deploy committed resources.
findings.figures: Amount not specified
findings.quote: ensure that the highways funding be fully carried forward rather than lost

findings.paper_title: Item 05(ii) References from Budget & Corp OSC 01.10.26
findings.headline: Approximately 30 per cent of Corporate Improvement and Savings Plan projects affected by slippage
findings.detail: The O&S Committee identified slippage in roughly one-third of the Corporate Improvement and Savings Plan projects. The Committee specifically requested the Head of Paid Service explain this issue, indicating material concern about delivery.
findings.matters: Only 70 per cent of planned improvement and savings projects are on track; significant delivery risk to whether the council's budget recovery plan will be achieved on schedule.

findings.quote: The slippage affecting approximately 30% of projects

findings.paper_title: Item 05(ii) References from Budget & Corp OSC 01.10.26
findings.headline: Revenue overspend in current year noted with concern
findings.detail: The O&S Committee considered the General Fund Budget Outturn and Capital Outturn and noted the revenue overspend with concern. This indicates the council exceeded its current-year budget despite savings initiatives.
findings.matters: A current-year revenue overspend signals loss of financial control and raises questions about the council's ability to manage within approved budgets.

findings.quote: Notes the revenue overspend with concern

findings.paper_title: Item 12.1 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn
findings.headline: Cleat Hill explosion response costs of £1.804 million remain unfunded after Bellwin scheme rejection
findings.detail: Expenditure of £1.804m was incurred responding to the Cleat Hill explosion, including gas monitoring costs. The council's application to the Bellwin Scheme was refused; the government directed it to pursue exceptional support. The costs were funded via EFS in 2025/26 but remain unfunded from permanent sources.
findings.matters: An emergency response cost of this scale (1% of annual revenue budget) is material; while currently covered via EFS, it represents an unresolved liability.
findings.figures: £1.804m response costs; EFS-funded in 2025/26
findings.quote: The Council applied to the national Bellwin Scheme for support from government in response to this unique event. The Government refused the application as their view was that the threshold had not been met within the time limit and directed the Council to apply for exceptional support

findings.paper_title: Item 12.1 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation demand grew 143% from 2022 to 2026 but growth rate decelerated to 2% in 2025/26
findings.detail: Temporary Accommodation households grew 143% from 377 (31 March 2022) to 918 (31 March 2026) but growth rate decelerated from 27% in 2023/24 to 2% in 2025/26. The council implemented targeted interventions including grant-funded prevention, improved case officer capacity, recruitment freeze, and in-house logistics service. The demand deceleration suggests these interventions are beginning to take effect.
findings.matters: TA is expensive; the deceleration in growth is rare positive news among councils managing housing pressures, suggesting targeted prevention and rehousing activity may be taking effect.
findings.figures: TA households 377 to 918 (143% growth); Peak growth 27% (2023/24); Growth 2% in 2025/26 (20 households)
findings.quote: The number of households in Temporary Accommodation has risen from 377 on 31 March 2022 to 918 on 31 March 2026. However as demonstrated in the following chart the rate of demand growth is slowing, from a peak of 27% growth in 2023/24 to a 2% growth (20 households) in 2025/26

findings.paper_title: Item 12.1 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn
findings.headline: Capital programme underspent by £40.470 million gross due to scheme slippage
findings.detail: The 2025/26 capital programme recorded gross underspend of £40.470m (32% of budget) due to slippage in Temporary Accommodation, Highways, Town Centre Regeneration, and Children's services schemes. Capital receipts achieved £7.542m against forecast £10.444m due to property sale delays. The underspent amounts are carried forward in the revised programme for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Programme slippage signals either forecasting issues or delivery challenges; large schemes addressing strategic priorities (Temporary Accommodation, school capacity) falling behind schedule has service and financial implications.
findings.figures: Gross underspend £40.470m (32% of £125.728m); Net underspend £19.517m; Capital receipts £7.542m vs forecast £10.444m

findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy claim shortfall of £2.606 million due to government policy on Supported Exempt Accommodation
findings.detail: Resources directorate overspent £1.849m, of which £2.606m was a housing benefit subsidy shortfall on Supported Exempt Accommodation and nightly let schemes. SEA placements generate approximately 44% loss on subsidy (average payable £327.49 against rent costs). An external review confirmed the shortfall is policy-driven and cannot be resolved without government policy change.
findings.matters: This is not a council efficiency problem; it is a structural policy gap that cannot be fixed internally and represents a recurring £2.6m annual cost exposure.

The amount of Housing Benefit Subsidy that can be claimed from the DWP for these claims is set by the Rent Officer Decision (independent of the Council) and is significantly below rent payable, with the average housing benefit payable per claim week being £327.49, there is a loss on the subsidy received of around 44%

findings.paper_title: Item 12.1 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn

findings.detail: Adult Services overspent by £3.207m (4% of budget), primarily due to external social care costs (£3.275m) reflecting higher placement costs, increased need complexity, and elevated care market prices. Charts show active client numbers plateaued but external care package costs rising significantly, indicating permanent shift to higher-complexity cases. The council reports beginning to see impacts of mitigations (preventative work, validation boards, package reviews) reducing cost increase trajectory.
findings.matters: Rising unit costs in adult social care amid stable or declining volumes typically signal permanent shift to higher-complexity cases, indicating structural cost pressures that reverse slowly.

findings.detail: Children's Services recorded £14.339m overspend (30% of budget), primarily on Looked After Children placements (£9.824m) driven by growth in LAC numbers, shift to expensive residential placements, and national placement insufficiency. findings.paper_title: Item 12.1 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn

findings.detail: Bedford finished 2025/26 with a 10% overspend (£17.726m against £177.616m budget) primarily due to demand pressures in children's and adult social care. The council drew £20m in 2025/26, with £4.078m balance carried forward to strengthen reserves.

findings.paper_title: Item 18 Pension Fund Update
findings.headline: Pension Schemes Act 2026 implemented new pooling and governance regulations effective 30 June 2026, transferring investment implementation responsibility to BCPP
findings.detail: The Pension Schemes Act 2026, enacted 29 April 2026, implemented government's Fit for the Future reforms through new regulations that came into force on 30 June 2026. From 1 July 2026, Border to Coast Pension Partnership became responsible for investment implementation decisions, with the Fund working with BCPP during a transitional phase to build necessary capabilities.
findings.matters: This represents a material change in how investment decisions are implemented and governed, affecting the Fund's governance structure, decision-making processes, and the relationship between the Fund and its investment pool.
findings.figures: 30 June 2026 (regulations effective date), 1 July 2026 (BCPP implementation responsibility begins), 29 April 2026 (Act enacted)
findings.quote: From 1 July 2026, under these new regulations, BCPP is responsible for investment implementation decisions.

findings.paper_title: Item 18 Pension Fund Update
findings.headline: Bedfordshire Pension Fund investment returned 16.6% for year to 30 June 2026, 0.6% below 17.2% composite benchmark
findings.detail: For the year to 30 June 2026, the Fund achieved a net aggregate annual return of 16.6%, 0.6% below the composite benchmark of 17.2%. The return exceeded the discount rate used by the actuary in determining liabilities, and the Fund has outperformed the discount rate for all reporting periods, contributing to the improved funding level at the 2025 valuation.
findings.matters: Investment performance is critical to fund sustainability and contribution rate setting; the Fund's modest underperformance against benchmark is not material to its overall strategy effectiveness, as demonstrated by strong valuation outcome.
findings.figures: 16.6% (annual return), 17.2% (composite benchmark), 0.6% (underperformance)
findings.quote: For the year to 30 June 2026, the Fund showed a net aggregate annual return of 16.6%, 0.6% behind the composite benchmark of 17.2%.

findings.paper_title: Item 18 Pension Fund Update
findings.headline: Bedfordshire Pension Fund now cash flow neutral on contributions and benefits, but marginally negative when administration costs included
findings.detail: Contributions from employees and employers are now broadly equal to pension payments, meaning the Fund is operationally cash flow neutral. However, when administration costs are included, cash flow projections are marginally negative. This reflects the ongoing maturation of the Fund's membership profile and means investment-generated cash will increasingly be required to support pension payments.
findings.matters: This structural shift signals that long-term fund sustainability depends increasingly on investment performance rather than contribution income, requiring continued strong fund stewardship and indicating critical dependency on investment returns.
findings.figures: Not quantified in document
findings.quote: The Fund has recently become cash flow neutral, with contribution income broadly equal to pension payments. However, when administration costs are taken into account, cash flow projections are marginally negative, meaning that investment-generated cash will increasingly be required to support pension payments.

findings.headline: Bedfordshire Pension Fund funding ratio improved from 92% (2022 valuation) to 102% (2025 valuation), resulting in contribution reductions for most employers
findings.detail: The 2025 triennial valuation concluded 31 March 2026. At the Fund level, the ratio of assets to liabilities improved from 92% at the 2022 valuation to 102% at the 2025 valuation, moving the Fund from underfunded to fully funded. This improvement resulted in a reduction in contributions for most participating employers.
findings.matters: Reduced pension contributions directly ease budget pressures for the council and participating employer bodies, providing significant financial relief and improving contribution rate predictability.
findings.figures: 92% (2022 Valuation), 102% (2025 valuation)
findings.quote: At the Fund level, the ratio of assets to liabilities has improved from 92% (2022 Valuation) to 102% at the 2025 valuation which has resulted in a reduction in contributions for most participating employers.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.2 Revenue and Capital Trends
findings.headline: Debt maturity profile rebalanced in July 2026 after breaching upper limit on short-term debt concentration
findings.detail: At 30 June, the council held debt with 50 per cent maturing within 12 months (above the 50% upper limit) and 67% within 3 years (above the 65% upper limit on the alternative indicator). The council converted short-term debt to longer-dated borrowing (5 and 10 year terms) in July, bringing the profile back within all prudential indicator boundaries by end-July.
findings.matters: Refinancing risk management is critical for local authority financial stability. A breach of the maturity indicator signals either front-loaded debt maturities or timing of new borrowing that could spike refinancing costs in a rising-rate environment. The swift corrective action is positive but a lender should understand what triggered the initial breach and whether it reflects debt management or a one-off timing issue.
findings.figures: At 30 June: 50% debt <12 months (limit 50% upper), 67% debt <3 years (limit 65% upper); long-term debt re-profiled in July to bring within limits
findings.quote: This shows that the Council held debt balances below the lower limit within the two to five year timeframe and also held a higher proportion of debt up to three years than the upper limit. Within July some short term debt was converted to long-term debt taken out over both a five and ten year duration and as at the end of July the debt profile was within all indicator boundaries.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.2 Revenue and Capital Trends
findings.headline: General Fund Reserve balance forecast at £15.949 million, within assessed adequate range of £14.6–£17.8 million
findings.detail: The General Fund Reserve opened at £14.199 million (1 April 2026, at lower end of the risk-assessed adequate range). The council has budgeted a contribution of £1.750 million, with no planned in-year use, giving a forecast closing balance of £15.949 million. This remains within the assessed range and provides cover, but growth is modest and leaves limited headroom above the minimum threshold.
findings.matters: Reserve adequacy is fundamental to financial resilience, particularly given the medium-term deficits forecast. A reserve at the lower-middle of an adequate range leaves limited buffer for adverse variance. A lender would assess whether the reserve trajectory can sustain the bridge to balanced budget.
findings.figures: Opening balance 1 Apr 2026: £14.199m; budgeted contribution: £1.750m; forecast closing balance: £15.949m; assessed adequate range: £14.6m–£17.8m
findings.quote: The General Fund Reserve balance as at 1 April 2026 is £14.199 million with a budgeted contribution to be made within 2026/27 of £1.750 million. The forecast closing balance of the General Fund Reserve is £15.949 million. This is within the current risk assessed range.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.2 Revenue and Capital Trends
findings.headline: Sundry debt arrears of £13.454 million outstanding beyond 91 days (18.23 per cent of amount collectable), with £10 million in adult social care
findings.detail: Total sundry debt outstanding at 30 June 2026 is £20.554 million (up from £18.736 million at start of year). Of this, £13.454 million has been outstanding longer than 91 days, representing a material risk of non-recovery. £10 million of the aged debt relates to adult social care, of which £4.7 million is awaiting probate (legally blocked). An Adult Services Debt Management Panel has been established and enforcement agent contract is being re-tendered with social value criteria.
findings.matters: Aged debt is a cash flow and reserve resilience issue. Adult social care debt is often complex (care charging, deprivation of assets, probate delays). A lender should understand recovery trajectory and impact on cash position.
findings.figures: Total sundry debt outstanding: £20.554m (up from £18.736m at start of year); aged debt >91 days: £13.454m (18.23% of collectable); ASC debt: £10m (of which £4.7m awaiting probate)

findings.paper_title: Item 12.2 Revenue and Capital Trends
findings.headline: Bereavement Services income shortfall of £0.460 million with mitigation plan to increase service duration and ground capacity
findings.detail: The council's bereavement services (cemeteries/cremations) are forecasting income below budget. Mitigation actions include benchmarking fees and charges against other facilities, extending service duration from 45 minutes to one hour (to reduce overruns and capacity constraints), and expanding ground space (identified land for 20 additional sanctums and a memorial garden). Progress will be tracked in future reports.
findings.matters: Bereavement services income can be volatile and demand-sensitive. The 45→60 minute change suggests a service design issue affecting throughput. A peer would want to know whether other councils have faced similar issues and what fee levels generate demand.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation numbers stabilizing at 910 placements (down from 921 in April 2026), following demand-led volatility
findings.detail: TA is a highly volatile demand-driven service; numbers had been under upward pressure. The council reports a downward movement in the quarter. TA is forecast with an underspend of £0.529 million within the Housing, Homelessness and Customer Contact directorate as a whole. The council is implementing cost-control measures: expanding council-owned TA, procuring nightly-rate accommodation to secure better value, and a digital programme to strengthen management and income recovery. The mix is 13% council-owned, 81% nightly-rate, and 5% hotel.
findings.matters: TA costs are demand-led and interact with housing benefit subsidy rules. A peer council would want to understand the mix of interventions (prevention, rehousing, accommodation type) driving the stabilisation. A lender should monitor whether the downward trend persists or is volatile.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.2 Revenue and Capital Trends
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant accumulated deficit of £1.678 million subject to 90 per cent DfE funding via High Needs Stability Grant, pending approval of SEND reform plan
findings.detail: The council submitted a local SEND reform plan to the Department for Education and was expecting approval notification by September 2026 (paper dated 30 Sept but does not confirm approval status). The DfE has committed to fund 90 per cent of the accumulated DSG deficit accrued to 31 March 2026 (£1.678 million), with funding from autumn 2026, conditional on plan approval. The statutory override allowing councils to carry DSG deficits expires at end 2027/28. Current-year High Needs Block forecast deficit is £8.412 million, driven by increases in EHCP numbers and complexity of need.
findings.matters: The DSG funding is time-limited and conditional; a lender needs to know the approval status and the path for deficits after 2027/28 when the override expires. The SEND reform plan affects spending trajectory in both directions: capital investment in local provision will incur revenue costs initially but should reduce high-cost independent school placements. The approval uncertainty creates a short-term contingency risk.
findings.figures: Accumulated DSG deficit to 31 Mar 2026: £1.678m (90% eligible for DfE grant); High Needs Block deficit £3.692m; current-year High Needs forecast deficit £8.412m; Experts at Hand grant £1.614m
findings.quote: The Department for Education (DfE) will be funding 90% of the accumulated deficit of the DSG to 31 March 2026 via the High Needs Stability Grant, with funding being made available from the Autumn of 2026. The funding is conditional on developing and submitting a local SEND reform plan, which is then approved as meeting the required criteria.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.2 Revenue and Capital Trends
findings.headline: Medium-term deficits of £32.1 million in 2027/28, cumulative £48.4 million by 2030/31, requiring further use of EFS and/or major savings delivery
findings.detail: The council's medium-term working assumptions show annual deficits continuing through the forecast period. The largest gap is in 2027/28 (£32.1 million), with additional smaller deficits in later years. These forecasts do not include use of EFS beyond 2027/28. The Executive approved a budget strategy in June 2026 committing not to exceed £10 million EFS beyond 2027/28, with the aim of eliminating EFS reliance beyond that point. Directorate savings targets have been set and the council is advancing earlier preparation of 2027/28 budget.
findings.matters: A council in this position faces binding choices between large tax rises, service cuts, or reserve depletion. The commitment to limit EFS signals awareness but the scale of the gap (£32m) is material relative to the council's net budget (£228m). A peer would want to understand what savings levers remain unimplemented. A lender would assess reserve adequacy and whether the medium-term plan is credible.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.2 Revenue and Capital Trends
findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy loss of £1.817 million on Supported Exempt Accommodation and short-term leases, driven by capped LHA rates not matching market rents
findings.detail: Supported Exempt Accommodation (SEA) claims have risen to 469 by June 2026 (from 371 in April 2025) with average weekly benefit payable up to £343.75. The government subsidy is capped at Broad Rental Market Area LHA rates, which have not been uplifted to match actual market rents; the loss on SEA is £1.185 million (47% of cost paid out). Short-term leased accommodation (used as temporary accommodation) shows £0.632 million loss (35% of cost), capped at 90% of the 2011 LHA rate. The council is lobbying the LGA and MPs on this issue.
findings.matters: This is a structural funding gap, not operational overspend. Other councils receiving similar LHA-capped subsidy will face identical pressures. A lender should understand whether the council views this as time-limited (pending government rate uplift) or a permanent draw on reserves or general fund.
findings.figures: SEA claims £1.185 million loss (47% of benefit paid); short-term lease loss £0.632 million (35% of benefit paid); SEA claims 469 (up from 371 April 2025); average weekly SEA benefit £343.75 (up from £279.91 April 2025)
findings.quote: Housing benefit subsidy claims for SEA properties to the end of June have therefore seen a loss compared to housing benefit paid out of £1.185 million equivalent to 47%.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.2 Revenue and Capital Trends
findings.headline: Looked After Children placements overspend of £3.139 million driven by increased residential placements, particularly in the 12–14 age group
findings.detail: Residential placements have increased significantly over the past two years, with higher volumes and higher costs per placement. LAC numbers increased in 2026/27 compared to 2025/26, although the rate of new entries is slowing (lowest for two years excluding Yarl's Wood impacts). The council is working to step down cohorts from residential to foster care, but has recruitment and approval constraints. Four new social workers joined in mid-August.

A lender needs to know whether this is a one-year spike or a persistent demand shift.

findings.matters: Three consecutive disclaimer opinions create reporting uncertainty and audit trail gaps, even if attributed to auditor rather than council issues; lenders assess financial reporting reliability partly through audit quality.

findings.paper_title: Item 14 Audit Committee Annual Report for Full Council - 2025-26

findings.detail: Staffing constraints affected operation of controls in some areas, availability of staff to support audits, and speed of implementing audit recommendations. Control actions included introduction of a Spending Management Panel for all commitments over £500 and a recruitment moratorium with removal of vacant posts.

findings.matters: When the external auditor flags finance team capacity as a risk to delivering core functions, it signals that control operation and decision-making quality may be compromised under current staffing.

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation caseload of 918 households has slowed its growth rate to 2% in 2025/26, from a peak of 27% in 2023/24, but absolute numbers remain high.
findings.detail: The number of households in temporary accommodation has grown from 377 on 31 March 2022 to 918 on 31 March 2026 — an increase of 543 households or 144% over four years. However, the rate of growth has decelerated significantly: 27% in 2023/24, then falling to 2% (20 additional households) in 2025/26. This slowing is attributed to actions taken including targeted grant funding for homelessness prevention, improved case officer capacity, recruitment freeze and controls on overtime, and a new in-house logistics and storage service that reduced spend on storage and taxis.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a high-cost demand pressure; while growth is slowing, the absolute numbers remain elevated and continue to drive revenue spend. Demonstrating decline in growth rate is a leading indicator of control, but absolute numbers suggest medium-term capital and revenue commitment.

findings.paper_title: Item 08 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn
findings.headline: General Fund reserve stands at £14.2 million, below the risk-assessed minimum of £14.6 million, and is expected to reach within range by March 2027.
findings.detail: The General Fund balance increased from £9.616m (31 March 2025) to £14.199m (31 March 2026) through a planned contribution of £1.750m plus an additional year-end contribution of £3.078m from unused EFS. The risk assessment has been updated and now recommends a range of £14.6m to £17.8m. The council projects the balance will reach £15.949m by 31 March 2027, within the range, subject to delivery of the Savings and Improvement Plans. A £1m Energy Resilience Reserve was created from the unused EFS balance due to turbulence in energy prices following the start of war in the Middle East in March 2026.
findings.matters: A reserve below the risk-assessed minimum indicates limited buffer for unexpected demand or cost pressures; council is dependent on delivery of savings plans to rebuild resilience within agreed timeframe.

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Item 08 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn
findings.headline: Housing benefit subsidy shortfall of £2.6 million, caused by government policy mismatch: Supported Exempt Accommodation subsidy averages 44% loss on actual rent paid.
findings.detail: The council is losing approximately 44% of actual rent cost on Supported Exempt Accommodation claims, as the subsidy amount is set by independent Rent Officer Decisions and is significantly below rent payable (average £327.49 per claim week). The same structural loss exists on nightly-let temporary accommodation where subsidy remains pegged to 2011 Local Housing Authority rates while rents have risen. An external review confirmed the technical expertise exists within the team but confirmed that without government policy change, the shortfall will persist. The Local Government Association has raised this with government.
findings.matters: This is a structural policy-driven loss, not manageable within council control; it will recur annually and signals a systematic underfunding of homelessness support across all councils using similar accommodation types.
findings.figures: £2.606 million overspend; average housing benefit payable £327.49 per claim week; 44% loss on subsidy received
findings.quote: The amount of Housing Benefit Subsidy that can be claimed from the DWP for these claims is set by the Rent Officer Decision (independent of the Council) and is significantly below rent payable, with the average housing benefit payable per claim week being £327.49, there is a loss on the subsidy received of around 44%. Without change to Government policy, the shortfall in Housing Benefit Subsidy will continue to be an issue.

findings.detail: Despite increases to the 2025/26 budget to reflect demand forecasts and care market cost inflation, external social care still overspent. The overspend reflects increases in levels of need, higher average hours agreed for home care packages, and spot price increases in supported living. The council notes that active clients have plateaued but those in care have more complex needs, driving higher support costs. Work is underway to manage trajectory through preventative services and the Thrive transformation project.
findings.matters: Adult social care demand is growing in cost per placement as clients present with greater complexity; this is a structural pressure rather than volume growth, suggesting limited opportunity for cost avoidance.

findings.detail: Operational spending reached £200.261m against a budget of £183.271m. Monthly monitoring and corporate controls including a Spending Management Panel, recruitment freezes, and agency staff reduction were in place throughout the year but did not prevent the overspend. The budget gap is attributed to demand pressures in social care placements, adult package costs, and housing support.
findings.matters: A 10% overspend indicates demand-driven cost pressures that built-in controls have not contained; this signals structural budget problems and dependency on exceptional support rather than sustainable management.

findings.quote: Demand in key areas continued to be a pressure resulting in a £17.726 million overspend, against the £177.616 million net budget, equivalent to 10%.

findings.paper_title: Item 08 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn
findings.headline: Council drew £20 million Exceptional Financial Support to cover structural budget deficit in 2025/26.
findings.detail: Bedford applied for £22m EFS in December 2025 to fund forecast deficit and Cleat Hill costs, and was notified on 23 February 2026 that the application had been accepted in principle. findings.matters: Policy-driven gaps between costs and recoverable subsidies create structural budget pressures; rising TA demand linked to welfare policy changes affects financial forecasts.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 - final draft 13 July 2026
findings.headline: Unmanageable structural budget deficit persists through 2029/30
findings.detail: The council forecasts a £27m budget gap in 2027/28 and cumulative £58.6m gap by 2029/30. Medium-Term Financial Strategy was not agreed during the year. Even with the planned improvement plan and savings, the structural deficit remains. Current projections show no clear path to eliminating government dependency.
findings.matters: Forecasted deficits this large cannot be closed by normal efficiency savings. They signal need for service reductions, asset sales, or ongoing exceptional support—all indicating governance failure.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 - final draft 13 July 2026
findings.headline: Reserves depleted to £14.2m, below recommended minimum, with no clear recovery path

findings.matters: Depleted reserves leave no buffer for demand shocks or unexpected pressures. Once exhausted, the council has no financial flexibility and cannot manage service disruptions.

findings.headline: Dependency on £58m exceptional support to avoid Section 114 Notice
findings.detail: The council received £22m Exceptional Financial Support for 2025/26 and requires £58m for 2026/27 (£25m revenue, £33m for Wixams Station risk). Without this government support, the council would have issued a Section 114 Notice. This dependency masks structural deficits that cannot be addressed without continued exceptional support or service cuts.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on repeated exceptional government support as sustainable funding. The council is operationally insolvent without government handouts, indicating the improvement plan has not yet stabilised the underlying position.

The auditor concluded there was a significant weakness because the Improvement Plan was not fully embedded in council operations as of March 2025, only being formally approved in January 2026.

findings.detail: For Investment Property, the auditor selected 10 items for testing but evidence was not provided for 3 of them, and floor area evidence was missing for all items. findings.headline: The finance team lacked sufficient capacity to meet statutory deadlines and audit obligations, causing delays in publishing financial statements
findings.detail: The council did not publish its unaudited financial statements by the 30 June 2025 statutory deadline because the initial draft was not of sufficient quality. The auditor identified this as a significant weakness: the finance team had insufficient capacity to undertake core objectives and respond to additional demands. Despite new appointments after year-end, the team remains stretched due to high demand for financial information. Some key reconciliations (payroll and Fixed Asset Register) required further work before audit could proceed.
findings.matters: Weak finance function capacity affects financial controls, timeliness of reporting, and audit quality. This compounds the audit risk, delays access to financial information needed for decision-making, and signals internal control deficiencies.

findings.detail: Facing the projected overspend, Bedford requested £90m across three financial years (2025-26 to 2027-28) from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. The requests for 2025-26 and 2026-27 were approved in principle on 23 February 2026. This requirement was only identified after the financial year ended, indicating plans developed during the year proved inadequate.
findings.matters: Exceptional Financial Support is a last-resort intervention used when a council cannot balance its budget. It signals the council lacks sufficient resources or cost control and depends on central government bailout. This materially affects the council's financial standing and independence.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 - Appendix A - Auditor’s Annual Report for Bedford Borough Council 202425
findings.headline: The council faces a projected £42.2m funding gap by 2029 and an £11.7m overspend in 2025-26 that would fully deplete available reserves
findings.detail: The September 2024 Medium-Term Financial Strategy forecast shows revenue spending will exceed available resources by £42.2m by the end of 2029 without additional action. In 2025-26, the council was forecasting a £11.7m overspend (by September 2025) against available general fund reserves of only £11.1m. This would fully exhaust reserves. The council has usable reserves have declined 44% since March 2022 (a £39.9m reduction).
findings.matters: A council that depletes reserves lacks a buffer for emergencies or volatility. The multi-year structural deficit signals the council cannot sustainably balance its budget and will require external support or service cuts. This is a clear solvency risk for lenders.
findings.figures: £42.2m gap by 2029; £11.7m September 2025 overspend; £11.1m available reserves; 44% reduction in usable reserves since March 2022
findings.quote: In September 2024, the Council updated the Medium-Term Financial Strategy for the four years to 2028/29. This report estimated that, without additional action, the gap between revenue spending and resources will grow to £42.2m by the end 2029. This is a clear risk to financial sustainability given the level of reserves available to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 - Appendix A - Auditor’s Annual Report for Bedford Borough Council 202425
findings.headline: Auditor issued a disclaimer of opinion on the council's financial statements, unable to obtain sufficient audit evidence on multiple critical areas

Key areas where evidence was unavailable include Property, Plant & Equipment valuations, Investment Property valuations, Employee benefits expenses, reserve movements, and comparative figures for 2024. This is the second consecutive year of disclaimer.
findings.matters: A disclaimer means the auditor cannot verify the accuracy of the council's reported financial position. This creates material uncertainty about the balance sheet and reserves available, directly affecting creditworthiness assessment and covenant compliance.
findings.figures: Disclaimer issued 26 February 2026; areas affecting £billion-scale assets and reserves unverified
findings.quote: We issued a disclaimer of opinion on the Council's financial statements on 26th February 2026. This is because we were unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn
findings.headline: Two exceptional items totalling £2.374 million pushed the council to seek exceptional financial support, revealing insufficient financial resilience for shocks.
findings.detail: The Cleat Hill gas explosion cost £1.804 million. The council applied to the Bellwin emergency scheme but was refused on technical grounds (threshold/timing); government directed application for EFS instead. The Wixams Station project, transferred to Network Rail, was subject to a cost review that reclassified £0.570 million from capital to revenue, requiring further EFS support. These events demonstrate the council lacks capacity to absorb one-off shocks.
findings.matters: Exceptional items are by definition unexpected. A well-capitalised council would absorb them from reserves. This council could not, signalling weak financial position prior to the shocks. The Wixams reclassification also flags governance risk: initial cost categorisation was incorrect.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation households increased from 377 on 31 March 2022 to 918 on 31 March 2026, with 2% growth in 2025/26
findings.detail: TA numbers have grown from 377 households on 31 March 2022 to 918 on 31 March 2026. Growth has slowed from a 27% peak in 2023/24 to 2% (20 households) in 2025/26, but the absolute level remains very high. The council is managing costs through targeted grant funding and a new in-house logistics service, but underlying demand is driven by housing market dysfunction and is exposed to economic shocks.
findings.matters: A TA population of 918 is a liability: it reflects both housing market conditions (outside the council's control) and the council's role as housing provider of last resort. These households are vulnerable to economic downturn and represent ongoing demand for homelessness services.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has grown to £1.678 million with the High Needs block now £3.692 million in deficit, driven by explosive growth in EHCP numbers.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit increased by £1.351 million in 2025/26, with the High Needs block deteriorating by £2.211 million due to growth in Education, Health and Care Plans. The government will fund 90% of the accumulated deficit by autumn 2026, but the remaining 10% and all future deficits remain subject to statutory override until 31 March 2028. High-needs spending is outpacing government grant allocation.
findings.matters: Growing EHCP numbers signal either unmet need in mainstream education or earlier identification of need. If the statutory override ends, the council will face a £1m+ annual liability. The growth rate is not within the council's control.
