findings.paper_title: Item 13 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn
findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy is structurally unaffordable: the council loses 44% on Supported Exempt Accommodation and the gap cannot be closed by operational efficiency.
findings.detail: The council overspent by £2.606 million on housing benefit subsidy due to government rate-setting policy. For Supported Exempt Accommodation, the Rent Officer Decision (independent of the council) sets subsidy rates far below actual rent: 'the average housing benefit payable per claim week being £327.49, there is a loss on the subsidy received of around 44%.' Nightly lets in Temporary Accommodation are subsidised at only 90% of the 2011 LHA rate. An external review confirmed the council has technical expertise but concluded 'without change to Government policy, the shortfall in Housing Benefit Subsidy will continue to be an issue.'
findings.matters: This is a policy-driven structural gap that operational improvements cannot close. It will persist until government changes subsidy methodology. It is a permanent drain on council finances.
findings.figures: £2.606m overspend; 44% loss on SEA subsidy claims; nightly lets at 90% of 2011 LHA rate
findings.quote: The average housing benefit payable per claim week being £327.49, there is a loss on the subsidy received of around 44%. The shortfall is also impacted by the Housing Benefit subsidy related to the use of nightly lets within Temporary Accommodation...without change to Government policy, the shortfall in Housing Benefit Subsidy will continue to be an issue.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn
findings.headline: Adults social care costs are rising faster than budgeted due to increasing client complexity and higher market spot prices, with preventative transformation not yet at scale.
findings.detail: External social care overspent by £3.275 million (6% on a £54.2m budget) due to 'increases in levels of need, increases in the average number of hours agreed for home care packages and higher spot prices in supported living.' The council describes clients receiving external packages as presenting with 'greater needs' and notes fewer opportunities for preventative intervention. Transformation via the Thrive project only commenced in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Rising care costs in an aging population suggest the council's budget assumptions are stale. Prevention work is starting late and at scale insufficient to offset growing demand. Future budgets may face similar pressures.
findings.figures: £3.275m overspend on external social care on £54.199m budget (6%)
findings.quote: There was an overspend in external social care of £3.275 million due to further increased cost of placements, due to increases in levels of need, increases in the average number of hours agreed for home care packages and higher spot prices in supported living.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn
findings.headline: General Fund reserve has fallen below the minimum risk-assessed threshold and offers insufficient protection against demand shocks.
findings.detail: As at 31 March 2026, the General Fund reserve stands at £14.199 million. The risk assessment recommends a range of £14.6 million to £17.8 million. The council plans to add £1.750 million in 2026/27 to reach £15.949 million by 31 March 2027, but this depends on delivering planned savings. The council notes the reserve 'would have been sufficient if the risk assessment had not been increased.'
findings.matters: A reserve below minimum threshold means the council lacks a buffer for demand shocks (like those materialising in children's and adults' services). Future resilience depends entirely on delivering savings targets, which are uncertain given the council's track record of overspending.
findings.figures: Current reserve £14.199m; minimum risk threshold £14.6m; target range £14.6m–£17.8m; planned 31 March 2027 £15.949m
findings.quote: A risk assessment of the General Fund Balance suggests that the reserve should be within the range of £14.6 million to £17.8 million. The General Fund as at 31 March 2026 stands at £14.202 million, below the minimum risk assessed value.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn
findings.headline: LAC placements overspent by £9.824m due to growth in residential placements, increased weekly costs, and breakdown of lower-cost alternatives
findings.detail: LAC placements overspent by £9.824 million, up £0.617m from December forecast. The council attributes this to 'growth in the number of residential placements, increase in weekly cost of placements and the complexity of need.' Lower-cost options (foster care, special guardianship) have 'broken down' due to case complexity. In 2026/27, the council is attempting to step down children to lower-cost care, but has only moved four children so far despite establishing a high-cost placements review meeting.
findings.matters: Worsening outcomes and rising costs suggest preventative work is failing. The pool of children requiring high-cost residential care is growing, not shrinking, indicating the council may lack capacity or early intervention capability to prevent escalation.
findings.figures: LAC placements £9.824m overspend; number of LAC increased 2025/26 vs 2024/25; four children stepped down in 2026/27 to date

findings.paper_title: Item 13 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn
findings.headline: The council is dependent on exceptional financial support (EFS) — a government capitalisation direction — which explicitly does not resolve underlying structural problems.
findings.detail: Bedford applied for £22 million of EFS in December 2025 and received approval for £20 million in revenue support plus £1.804 million for Cleat Hill. EFS allows the council to treat day-to-day revenue costs as capital, creating temporary breathing room. However, the government's own guidance states this 'creates short-term flexibility' while 'structural mitigation is delivered through an Improvement Plan, but does not resolve the underlying financial challenges.'
findings.matters: EFS is a one-off relief that defers problems rather than solving them. A council needing £20m+ in exceptional support cannot balance its budget sustainably and will require either future service cuts, income growth, or further government intervention.
findings.figures: £20m EFS approved for revenue; £1.804m EFS for Cleat Hill; £4.078m EFS balance carried forward; application made December 2025
findings.quote: EFS allows Councils to pay for certain costs by the Government issuing a capitalisation direction, which temporarily allows the Council to treat some day to day (revenue) costs as capital expenditure. This creates short-term flexibility, while structural mitigation is delivered through an Improvement Plan, but does not resolve the underlying financial challenges.

findings.paper_title: Item 13 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn

These are not one-off pressures but reflect demand growth and rising unit costs in care markets that the council's budgets have failed to anticipate or absorb.
findings.matters: A 10% structural overspend on the general fund indicates the council's core budgets are fundamentally broken. It signals ongoing financial stress and dependency on external support or reserve drawdown to balance.
findings.figures: £17.726m overspend on £177.616m net budget; Children's £14.339m on £47.339m; Adults £3.207m on £72.550m

findings.paper_title: Item 3 Section 25 Report

findings.detail: The council achieved 82% of planned savings in 2024/25 but only 56% in 2025/26. This is partly due to unachieved savings being reset, but fundamentally shows that savings are becoming harder to deliver as demand pressures override plans. The Improvement Plan requires 'pace' but staff capacity is 'already stretched' while 'significant headcount reductions are planned.'

findings.paper_title: Item 3 Section 25 Report

findings.detail: A separate capitalisation direction was made for an emergency that cost £2m. MHCLG refused both Bellwin Scheme funding and alternative support. The council continues to lobby but has no resolution or funding source secured.
findings.matters: This is an unfunded cost sitting on the council's books. It shows that government support cannot be relied on for emergencies outside SEND and is being actively negotiated rather than resolved.
findings.figures: Cleat Hill Emergency costs: £2.0 million; Bellwin Scheme funding: rejected
findings.quote: a further capitalisation direction was made in relation to the Cleat Hill Emergency, following the rejection by MHCLG to fund the £2.0 million costs incurred from the Bellwin Scheme or provide any other alternative funding.

findings.paper_title: Item 3 Section 25 Report
findings.headline: CIPFA Resilience Index places Bedford's reserves in the bottom quartile of peer comparator councils
findings.detail: An independent resilience review was commissioned, which concluded the council faces significant medium-term financial challenges and should develop a single Improvement Plan. The council is now structured with an Independent Improvement and Assurance Panel to drive delivery, but the underlying position remains weak.
findings.matters: This independent assessment confirms the council's financial position is materially weaker than similar authorities. It suggests systemic issues beyond the current cycle.
findings.figures: Reserves ranked in bottom quartile vs. primary comparator group
findings.quote: The CIPFA Resilience Index highlights that the level of reserves is in the bottom quartile compared to its primary comparator group.

findings.paper_title: Item 3 Section 25 Report
findings.headline: DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit will reach £4 million by March 2026; cumulative national deficit projected at £14 billion by 2028
findings.detail: The statutory override masking DSG deficits expires 2028/29. If government does not assume funding of SEND costs, councils will need to address accumulated deficits from reserves. The council believes the government should fund both ongoing costs and legacy deficits; without this, further savings would be needed.
findings.matters: This is a time-bomb in the sector. At March 2028 when the override expires, this council and many others face a choice between a Section 114 notice or finding £4m+ in new savings. It is a systemic solvency risk.
findings.figures: Bedford DSG deficit by March 2026: £4m additional debt; National cumulative deficit by March 2028: approximately £14 billion; Statutory override expires 2028/29
findings.quote: Recent sector surveys suggest that, without Government intervention, most councils would be unable to set a balanced budget and may need to issue a Section 114 notice; and this Council would need to review the level of EFS required.

findings.paper_title: Item 3 Section 25 Report
findings.headline: Capital receipts target of £27.5 million for 2026/27 is described as 'ambitious' with 'significant risk' given historical delays
findings.detail: The council is heavily dependent on asset sales to fund transformation costs. However, past performance shows 'significant delays due to the complexity of contracts, planning requirements and staff capacity.' Weekly tracking meetings are in place but the risk remains unresolved.
findings.matters: If capital receipts do not materialise, the council will need to borrow more or cut investments. This is a key delivery risk in the financial plan.
findings.figures: Planned capital receipts for 2026/27: £27.5m; This funds transformation and capital programme; Risk mitigation through RAG-rating discounts applied to receipts
findings.quote: The delivery of planned Capital Receipts from the sale of surplus assets is vital to the delivery of the Improvement Plan... The value and volume of sales planned in 2026/2027 of £27.5 million is ambitious and presents a significant risk.

findings.paper_title: Item 3 Section 25 Report
findings.headline: Planned borrowing will increase from £104 million to £227 million by March 2028, raising financing costs to 6.5% of net revenue
findings.detail: The council is planning a 118% increase in total borrowing over two years. Long-term borrowing increased from near-zero a year ago to £61m. The Treasury Management Panel has raised concerns about the overall borrowing level. This assumes no new capital requirements emerge.
findings.matters: This is a significant structural shift in the council's balance sheet. It increases revenue exposure to interest rate movements and locks in ongoing financing costs when the council is already struggling to fund services.
findings.figures: Current borrowing (31 Dec 2025): £104m; Planned maximum by 31 March 2028: £227m; Financing costs rise from 5.5% (2026/27) to 6.5% before falling in 2030/31; Long-term borrowing: £61m
findings.quote: Total borrowing is planned to increase from the current £104 million at 31 December 2025 to a maximum £227 million by 31 March 2028. This will move the proportion of financing costs to net revenue stream from 5.5% estimated in 2026/2027 to 6.5%.

findings.paper_title: Item 3 Section 25 Report
findings.headline: General Fund Reserve at £11.1 million is below the recommended risk-assessed range of £12.8-£15.6 million
findings.detail: The council's primary liquidity buffer is already depleted and below safe levels. Even after the 2025/26 outturn and assuming EFS approval, reserves are only projected to recover to £12.7m by 31 March 2026, still near the minimum. Total reserves fell from £28.2m to £25.9m forecast.
findings.matters: Low reserves mean the council has almost no capacity to absorb shocks or unforeseen cost pressures. It is already dependent on government support and has minimal flexibility.
findings.figures: Current General Fund Balance: £11.1m; Recommended range: £12.8-£15.6m; Projected 31/3/2026: £12.7m; Total reserves 31/3/2026 forecast: £25.9m (down from £28.2m)
findings.quote: The General Fund Balance currently stands at £11.1 million which is below the recommended range... this reduces the flexibility the Council has to re-prioritise to manage shocks when necessary.

findings.paper_title: Item 3 Section 25 Report
findings.headline: Current year (2025/26) overspend reached £14.3 million by end November with spending controls in place
findings.detail: Despite active spending controls on recruitment, agency staff and discretionary spend, the council is tracking to a £14.3m overspend. This is driven by demand-led pressures in social care and temporary accommodation that exceeded budget assumptions set in February 2025. The General Fund Reserve is insufficient to absorb this.
findings.matters: Shows that even with active controls in place, demand pressures are overriding budget discipline. This year ends March 2026 and the position will feed into reserves and future year borrowing.
findings.figures: £14.3m overspend forecast as at end November 2025; was £11.4m as at 30 September 2025
findings.quote: The latest reported position as at 30 September 2025 showed a £11.4 million overspend. This has risen to £14.3 million at the end of November.

findings.paper_title: Item 3 Section 25 Report
findings.headline: Council cannot set a balanced budget without up to £25 million in government Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: The council has applied for a capitalisation direction to fund revenue costs through borrowing and capital receipts. The S151 Officer states that if EFS is not approved by end February 2026, they would be duty-bound to issue a Section 114 notice, which would trigger government intervention and require consideration of further savings.
findings.matters: This is the single largest financial constraint on the council. Without approval, it cannot legally set a budget and would enter statutory intervention.
findings.figures: Up to £25 million capitalisation direction requested; £20 million EFS application submitted 12 December 2025
findings.quote: Based on the financial position in 2025/2026 and forecast budget gap for 2026/27 it is clear the Council is not able to set a balanced budget for 2026/2027 without the need for EFS.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1 Summary General Fund Revenue Budget 2026-2027
findings.headline: The Funding Formula contingency has been reduced by £336,000, with remaining reserves limited to managing business rate changes only.
findings.detail: The council reduced contingency by £336,000 to fund specific investments. The remaining reserve is 'set aside for business rate changes', leaving minimal flexibility to absorb unforeseen costs or in-year demand pressures during 2026/27.
findings.matters: A depleted contingency leaves the council vulnerable to in-year shocks and reduces its ability to respond to unexpected pressures without further borrowing.
findings.figures: £336,000 reduction in Funding Formula contingency
findings.quote: This facilitates a reduction to the Funding Formula contingency by £336,000 to fund the items above. The remaining reserve is set aside for business rate changes.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1 Summary General Fund Revenue Budget 2026-2027
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation households have risen from 897 to 919 since April 2025, increasing budget pressure on this statutory duty.
findings.detail: The paper explicitly states the budget was achieved without reducing TA numbers despite cost pressures, and the council maintains its statutory duty to accommodate under section 188 of the Housing Act. This 2.5% rise in nine months indicates ongoing structural demand growth.
findings.matters: Homelessness is an unfunded demand-led statutory duty that cannot be controlled through savings and will continue to place upward pressure on future budgets.
findings.figures: 897 households April 2025; 919 households January 2026
findings.quote: The budget position has been achieved without reductions in temporary accommodation household numbers which have actually risen from 897 in April 2025 to 919 in January 2026

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1 Summary General Fund Revenue Budget 2026-2027
findings.headline: Children's Services funding is inadequate without a £1.6 million contingency reserve, with an additional £1 million dependent on EFS approval.
findings.detail: The paper records concerns from councillors that Children's Services funding is insufficient. A £1.6 million reserve was established in 2025/26 for service pressures, with a further £1 million proposed from EFS. The Director acknowledges the budget is adequate only 'not withstanding any significant peaks in demand', indicating vulnerability to demand spikes.
findings.matters: Children's Services is a major demand-led budget line. The need for contingency reserves signals the council lacks confidence in its baseline funding for this service.
findings.figures: £1.6 million reserve established 2025/26; additional £1 million from EFS
findings.quote: Concerns have been raised across the Chamber that the amount allowed for Children's Services is not sufficient. A reserve has been established alongside the Children's Services Budget to allow for pressures of £1.6 million.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.1 Summary General Fund Revenue Budget 2026-2027
findings.headline: The council cannot set a balanced 2026/2027 budget without government Exceptional Financial Support, with revenue expenditure exceeding available income by £25 million.
findings.detail: Revenue expenditure of £228.045 million exceeds available income, requiring £25 million to be capitalized through EFS. The council applied for EFS in December 2025 with a decision expected by end-February 2026. The council expects to need EFS support for a minimum of three consecutive years (2025/26 through 2027/28).
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can independently balance its budget. Bedford's structural reliance on discretionary government support indicates fundamental financial weakness and creates approval risk.
findings.figures: £228.045 million revenue expenditure; £25 million deficit 2026/27; EFS requests: £20m (2025/26), £25m (2026/27), £10m (2027/28)
findings.quote: Full Council note the reliance of the 2026/2027 Budget on an application to the Ministry of Exceptional Financial Support, the outcome of which will be known by the end of February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.4 Capital Programme Update
findings.headline: Net borrowing requirement of £121.4 million over ten years, with revenue financing costs projected to reach 6.5% of net revenue stream in 2028/29.
findings.detail: After capital receipts, the council requires £121.356m net borrowing to fund the capital programme. Of this, £44.980m is classified as Invest-to-Save. Prudential indicators show financing costs rising to £16.109m (6.5% of net revenue stream) in 2028/29, then moderating. The council notes that increased borrowing will increase revenue costs 'falling on Council Tax'.
findings.matters: A doubling of capital financing costs as a proportion of revenue stream indicates rising debt service pressure; the council is explicitly flagging the Council Tax impact of this borrowing trajectory.
findings.figures: £121.356m net borrowing (2025/26–2034/35); financing costs £10.339m (2025/26) rising to £16.109m (2028/29); 5.1% to 6.5% of net revenue stream
findings.quote: The Council relies on borrowing to fund capital investment where there is no other source of funding and this has a direct impact on the revenue budget. The level of borrowing is a factor that needs to be considered by the Council as increased borrowing will increase the associated revenue costs and as such will fall on Council Tax.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.4 Capital Programme Update
findings.headline: £28.9 million of Flexible Capital Receipts policy being deployed to fund transformation costs required to deliver 2026/27 savings plan.
findings.detail: The programme includes £28.927m in investment from Flexible Capital Receipts to deliver the 'savings proposed in the 2026/2027 Budget' and to support delivery of an Improvement Plan through 2029/30. Detailed table shows £24.992m in redundancy and specialist resources across multiple directorates. This represents upfront transformation investment to achieve ongoing savings.
findings.matters: Significant upfront redundancy and transformation spend (£24.992m investment for £26.926m cumulative savings) indicates structural service restructuring is underway; execution risk on achieving savings is material.
findings.figures: £28.927m Flexible Capital Receipts deployment; £24.992m total investment for £26.926m cumulative savings target across 2026–2030
findings.quote: The scheme has been updated to reflect the cost of investment to deliver the savings proposed in the 2026/2027 Budget and to reflect investment to support the delivery of the Improvement Plan through to 2029-2030.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.4 Capital Programme Update
findings.headline: Discretionary capital schemes being terminated due to financial position.
findings.detail: Executive Decision 1851 terminated the Partnership Schemes in Conservation Areas (PSICA) Tavistock Improvement Scheme 'due to the financial position of the Council' (capital funding no longer viable). This discretionary scheme cancellation reflects ongoing pressure to prioritize spending.
findings.matters: Cancellation of previously-approved discretionary investment signals prioritization of essential services and ongoing austerity, relevant to demand and service sustainability.
findings.figures: PSICA Tavistock scheme terminated (amount not itemized separately in appendices)
findings.quote: Executive Decision 1851 was issued to terminate the Partnership Schemes in Conservation Areas (PSICA) Tavistock Improvement Scheme Due to the financial position of the Council, the capital funding for this discretionary scheme is no longer viable.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.4 Capital Programme Update
findings.headline: Community Infrastructure Levy receipts halved in latest forecast, requiring reprofilings of dependent schemes.
findings.detail: CIL receipts in 2025/26 came in significantly lower than anticipated, prompting a reduction in future-year projections from £4m per annum to £2m. The Primary Care Estate Scheme was reprofiled to 2028/29 to match anticipated CIL availability, though the report states this is not expected to impact delivery.
findings.matters: Downward revision of revenue forecasts mid-programme signals forecasting reliability issues and forces scheme replanning, affecting delivery timelines.
findings.figures: CIL projection reduced from £4m per annum to £2m per annum; £9.023m CIL still unallocated after 2028/29
findings.quote: The CIL receipts received in this year have been significantly lower than anticipated. Therefore, the projection for future year receipts has been reduced from £4 million per annum to £2 million.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.4 Capital Programme Update
findings.headline: Council has not achieved good track record delivering capital receipts; £101.403m of planned disposals forecast 2025/26–2034/35 underpins entire capital programme
findings.detail: The risk section explicitly states: 'The Council does not have a good track record in delivering capital receipts and this will continue to need close management.' The entire capital programme relies on £101.4m capital receipts; if these are not delivered or delayed, schemes must be removed or deferred 'to ensure that borrowing does not spiral'. Timing differences between receipts and expenditure will require careful cash management.
findings.matters: Capital receipt shortfalls force councils to either cut investment or increase borrowing; a poor track record of delivery creates material variance risk for lenders evaluating debt sustainability.
findings.figures: £101.403m capital receipts forecast 2025/26–2034/35; £54.907m from asset sales and £46.496m from disaggregation receipts
findings.quote: The Council does not have a good track record in delivering capital receipts and this will continue to need close management. If and when receipts are removed from the Programme then the expenditure should also be removed and/or delayed to ensure that borrowing does not spiral.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.4 Capital Programme Update
findings.headline: Wixams Station contract termination creates uncertain impairment loss, with £33 million held as contingency pending design completion.
findings.detail: Bedford terminated its contract with Network Rail in August 2025 following announcement of a Department for Transport 4-platform station. Costs already incurred do not benefit the new scheme and would require a Capitalisation Direction to avoid being a revenue cost. The council prudently provisioned the entire £33m forecast cost in the EFS application because final cost estimates will not be available until late 2026/27.
findings.matters: A major capital project write-down, even if hedged through EFS, signals project governance and due diligence risks, and the impairment loss represents unbudgeted financial exposure.
findings.figures: £33 million held in EFS application; final cost estimate unavailable until later 2026/27
findings.quote: The cancellation of the project may result in an impairment loss where costs already incurred do not benefit the new 4-platform station. Such costs would need to be counted as a revenue cost without a Capitalisation Direction.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.4 Capital Programme Update
findings.headline: Council requires £57 million in Exceptional Financial Support from government to balance its budget for 2026/27 and beyond.
findings.detail: Bedford has applied for £57m EFS across three years: £20m (2025/26), £25m (2026/27), and £10m (2027/28). The application is described as necessary to 'set a legal balanced budget for 2026/2027' and reflects the council's 'difficult financial position'. A further application is anticipated for 2027/28.
findings.matters: A council requiring exceptional government support to meet its legal balance budget obligation signals deep structural budget problems that lenders must factor into risk assessment.
findings.figures: £57 million EFS across 2025/26–2027/28 (£20m, £25m, £10m respectively)
findings.quote: as a result of the Council's difficult financial position, an application has been made to the Ministry for Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) for the current financial year, and this is required to set a legal balanced budget for 2026/2027

findings.paper_title: Item 4.3 Appendix A - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Asset disposal programme designed to fund EFS and transformation, creating execution risk
findings.detail: Council has undertaken a 'focussed review of assets' to raise capital receipts. Projected receipts for 2025/26 are £10.444m. If asset sales slip, the capital programme and potentially EFS funding could be affected.
findings.matters: Revenue support now depends partly on asset sales working as planned. Market conditions can affect property sale timings and values.
findings.figures: Projected capital receipts 2025/26: £10.444m
findings.quote: A focussed review of assets has been undertaken to deliver capital receipts to fund the Flexible Capital Receipts Programme and Exceptional Financial Support. Assets that do not make the required financial return will also be considered for sale.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.3 Appendix A - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Council planning £26.926m in annual savings (£85m cumulative) to balance a revised budget
findings.detail: The council is committing £24.992m upfront investment over 4 years to deliver transformation savings. Large savings programmes often slip. If this one does, the budget will be in deficit—and there is limited reserve headroom to absorb slippage.
findings.matters: Lenders need confidence that large savings programmes will land. Slippage would expose the council's underlying structural deficit. The £26.9m figure is material relative to overall budget.
findings.figures: 2026/27: £13.366m investment, targeting £10.948m savings. Cumulative investment £24.992m over 4 years; cumulative savings target £85.026m
findings.quote: The proposed 2026/2027 – 2029-30 Revenue Budget includes savings of £26.926 million, a proportion of which require an up-front investment to deliver. Therefore, with the extension of the policy, the Council proposes to fund £24.992 million of revenue costs to fund transformation. The cumulative saving to be generated from these proposals totals £85.026 million over the 4 years

findings.paper_title: Item 4.3 Appendix A - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing 21.9% in one year, with borrowing headroom nearly exhausted
findings.detail: CFR rises from £219.272m to £267.111m (2025/26 to 2026/27). Authorised borrowing limit increased from £170m to £225m. Council explicitly states 'there is little to no internal borrowing headroom'—meaning it has almost no flexibility to borrow more without requesting further limit increases.
findings.matters: This shows the council approaching its debt capacity. Limited headroom means it cannot absorb further capital needs or revenue pressures without additional approval.
findings.figures: CFR 2025/26: £219.272m; 2026/27: £267.111m. Authorised limit 2026/27: £225m (borrowing only)
findings.quote: The proposed Borrowing Limits have been increased to reflect the current financial situation, and that there is little to no internal borrowing headroom.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.3 Appendix A - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Council has shifted from cash-generative to net short-term borrower
findings.detail: Historically the council had cash available. It now borrows short-term to fund day-to-day operations and is planning a shift to long-term borrowing. Treasury strategy is explicitly moving away from liquidity management.
findings.matters: This reflects deteriorating cash position and increasing reliance on debt. A council that was self-funding is now dependent on capital markets.
findings.figures: Current borrowing: £104.873m at 4.40% average rate; treasury investments: £41.839m
findings.quote: The Council's cashflow has changed from typically having cash available to being a net short-term borrower as well as long-term borrower where capital expenditure is incurred before being financed.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.3 Appendix A - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Reserves are being drawn down to fund the revenue budget
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that borrowing limit increases have been driven by 'the increasing requirement to fund the revenue budget and reducing reserves and balances.' This is unsustainable—reserves are a buffer, not a budget funding source.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion signals structural budget problems. When reserves are exhausted, the council has no cushion for unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls.
findings.figures: No specific reserve figures given, only that balances are 'reducing'
findings.quote: This has been driven by the increasing requirement to fund the revenue budget and reducing reserves and balances.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.3 Appendix A - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: 2026/27 revenue budget depends entirely on unconfirmed Exceptional Financial Support from central government
findings.detail: The budget is predicated on a capitalisation direction from MHCLG. EFS approval must be confirmed by late February 2026. If not granted, the council faces a significant budget hole with no fallback.
findings.matters: This is a material and immediate risk to the council's financial sustainability. A lender needs to know the budget rests on approval expected days before Council approval.
findings.figures: EFS decision due 'late February 2026'; meeting is 18 February 2026
findings.quote: The 2026/2027 Revenue Budget is predicated on support through a capitalisation direction from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. EFS is subject to approval which be confirmed as part of the Final Local Government Settlement in late February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2 Treasury Strategy Covering Report 2026 2027
findings.headline: Capital programme expansion to £121.3 million over ten years requiring increased borrowing limits.
findings.detail: The proposed capital programme for 2026/2027 is £54.0 million, totalling £121.3 million over the 10-year programme after capital receipts. The document states it is inevitable that additional medium to longer term borrowing will be required and that borrowing limits must be increased.
findings.matters: Additional capital borrowing on top of existing revenue-driven borrowing increases total debt servicing burden and refinancing risk, particularly if revenue position does not improve.
findings.figures: £54.0 million 2026/27, £121.3 million over 10-year programme
findings.quote: Although the Capital Receipts Programme has been expanded over the last few years it is inevitable that additional medium to longer term borrowing will be required to fund the Capital Programme over the coming years, and that borrowing limits reflected in the Capital Strategy will need to be increased.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2 Treasury Strategy Covering Report 2026 2027
findings.headline: Pooled investment funds (£4.71% yield) under review for divestment to reduce borrowing.
findings.detail: Due to changing financial situation and the need to borrow, the council is reviewing long-term pooled investments made in 2015/2016 to potentially divest where there is no capital loss. No redemption has been included in prudential indicators as no decision is taken yet. This signifies the council may convert investments to cash to reduce debt.
findings.matters: Divesting strategic long-term investments to reduce borrowing indicates asset quality concerns and prioritisation of debt reduction over revenue diversification.
findings.figures: Current holdings yielding annualised return of 4.71%
findings.quote: Given the Council's changing financial situation, and need to borrow it is appropriate to review these pooled funds, where there is no loss of capital value to reduce borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2 Treasury Strategy Covering Report 2026 2027
findings.headline: £25 million capital spending required to pump-prime revenue budget savings over three years.
findings.detail: The council's Flexible Capital Receipts Programme has been expanded to fund pump-priming costs for delivering revenue budget savings and its improvement plan. This £25m spend over three years has been incorporated into treasury management assumptions, indicating the council needs significant capital investment to achieve revenue savings.
findings.matters: The need for substantial capital spending to deliver revenue savings is unusual and suggests underlying service cost challenges that cannot be resolved through efficiency alone.
findings.figures: £25 million over three years
findings.quote: The Capital Programme also includes a significant update to the Flexible Capital Receipts Programme to fund the pump-priming cost to deliver the revenue budget savings and the Council's Improvement Plan of £25 million over three years.

findings.paper_title: Item 4.2 Treasury Strategy Covering Report 2026 2027
findings.headline: Currently borrowing to cover revenue deficits and drawing reserves, seeking government exceptional financial support to reverse this.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that borrowing is currently being driven by revenue overspends and is depleting reserves. It has applied to MHCLG for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) totalling £20.0m (2025/26) and £25.0m (2026/27) for revenue budget support. The council says EFS approval would reverse the current position of revenue-driven borrowing and reserve depletion.
findings.matters: A council borrowing to cover day-to-day spending deficits (not investment) is in structural financial difficulty and signals high refinancing risk.
findings.quote: The recognition of EFS, if approved, should reverse the current position where borrowing is being driven revenue overspends and reducing reserves.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.1 Annual Treasury Outturn Report 2024-2025
findings.headline: Long-term pooled fund investments carry £2.657m unrealised loss, with statutory accounting override expiring 31 March 2029
findings.detail: The council holds £35m in pooled funds (equities, bonds, property, REITs). These showed a net unrealised loss of £2.657m as of 31 March 2025, down from £2.993m the prior year. Crucially, these losses are not currently charged to the General Fund due to a statutory override under SI 2018 No. 1207, but this override expires on 31 March 2029. After that date, unrealised losses will hit the revenue account and General Fund.
findings.matters: The council's General Fund is currently sheltered from investment volatility by a temporary accounting override; when this expires, future downturns in the £35m pooled fund portfolio could trigger significant revenue charges and impact reserves or require spending cuts.
findings.figures: £35m pooled fund investments held; £2.657m unrealised loss 31 March 2025; statutory override deadline 31 March 2029
findings.quote: The overall unrealised loss on Long Term Assets, for the reasons discussed above, was an unrealised loss of £2.657 million as of 31 March 2025

findings.paper_title: Item 12.1 Annual Treasury Outturn Report 2024-2025
findings.headline: Last-minute amendments to Capital Programme not reflected in Liability Benchmark; £2.2m Highways scheme amendment not included
findings.detail: The Capital Programme was changed on the day of publication, creating an inconsistency between the Capital Programme and the Liability Benchmark that will not be corrected until the mid-year report. A £2.2m amendment to the Highways BBC Funded Scheme could not be included in the updated Liability Benchmark. This suggests weak financial planning controls and forecasting processes.
findings.matters: Inconsistencies between capital and treasury plans, and changes at last minute after reports are prepared, indicate weak project governance and forecast reliability; a lender cannot rely on the council's spending plans.
findings.figures: £2.2m Highways scheme amendment; significant unnamed Capital Programme amendment on day of publication
findings.quote: a last-minute change to the Capital Programme on the day of publication has meant there is an inconsistency between the two documents that will need to be updated in the mid-year report.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.1 Annual Treasury Outturn Report 2024-2025
findings.headline: Treasury Management Panel initially rejected recommendation; report approved only by Executive three months later after updating forecasts
findings.detail: The report was presented to the Treasury Management Panel on 17 July 2025 and was not approved for recommendation. The panel flagged missing liability benchmark figures and outdated forecasts. The report was then approved by the Executive on 15 October 2025 after the Statement of Accounts was published, but only after forecasts were updated. This three-month delay and governance failure suggests concerns about data quality and council readiness.
findings.matters: A lender should be concerned that the council's own treasury panel did not have confidence in the numbers and forecasts; the three-month delay to update figures after year-end is unusual and suggests internal processes broke down.
findings.figures: Panel meeting 17 July 2025, Executive approval 15 October 2025 (3-month delay)
findings.quote: This report was considered by the Treasury Management Panel on 17 July 2025 and was not approved for recommendation. The Executive approved the report at its meeting on 15 October 2025.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.1 Annual Treasury Outturn Report 2024-2025
findings.headline: Four out of seven maturity structure prudential indicators breached; 64% of borrowing maturing within 12 months
findings.detail: The council breached maturity limits on borrowing under 12 months (64% actual vs 50% upper limit), 5-10 years (9% actual vs minimum 10% required), 10-20 years (0% vs 10% minimum), and 30-50 years (7% actual vs 10% minimum). The £79.9m short-term borrowing outstanding had an average maturity of just 14 days, creating acute rollover risk.
findings.matters: Concentration of debt maturity in the next 12 months at high rates exposes the council to refinancing risk; if rates spike or credit conditions tighten, the council will struggle to roll over this debt on affordable terms.
findings.figures: Under 12 months: 83,724 (64% of fixed rate borrowing, limit 0-50%); 5-10 years: 11,293 (9%, minimum 10%); 10-20 years: 0 (minimum 10%); average term of short-term borrowing 14 days at 5.84%
findings.quote: Short-Term Borrowing taken during 2024/2025 which was outstanding as at 31 March 2025 is £79.893 million with an average term of 14 days at an average rate of 5.84%

findings.paper_title: Item 12.1 Annual Treasury Outturn Report 2024-2025
findings.headline: Interest payments overran budget by £1.993m (93% overspend) due to short-term borrowing
findings.detail: Budgeted interest payable was £2.151m but actual was £4.144m. The council capitalised £1.253m of interest on two capital projects, which reduced the accounting charge but does not reduce the actual cash cost. The overspend reflects the council taking on significantly more short-term borrowing at higher rates than anticipated.
findings.matters: An unbudgeted interest cost of nearly £2m signals either poor cash forecasting or financial stress requiring urgent borrowing; indicates budget control weakness.
findings.figures: Budget £2.151m, Outturn £4.144m, Variance £1.993m; capitalised interest £1.253m
findings.quote: Interest Payable increased due to short term borrowing throughout reflecting the changing financial position of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.1 Annual Treasury Outturn Report 2024-2025
findings.headline: Total external debt of £130m deemed very high by Treasury Management Advisory Committee
findings.detail: External debt increased sharply from £88.4m (31 March 2024) to £130.1m (31 March 2025), a 47% increase year-on-year. The Treasury Management Advisory Committee explicitly raised concerns about this level of borrowing at their July 2025 meeting. The composition shifted dramatically towards Local Authority short-term borrowing (£79.9m at 31 March 2025).
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand why debt doubled and whether the council has a plan to manage or reduce it; sustained high debt limits financial flexibility and increases default risk.
findings.figures: £130.065m external debt 31 March 2025 vs £88.422m 31 March 2024; £79.893m short-term borrowing at average 14 days maturity at 5.84%
findings.quote: The Treasury Management Advisory Committee at their meeting on 17 July 2025 expressed concerns in relation to the total external debt having been £130million at the year end and this was deemed to be very high.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 Budget Preparation Process 2026-2027 - Savings Proposals for Consultation Phase 2 - Final
findings.headline: A spending control panel authorising all expenditure over £500 has been introduced to restrict discretionary departmental spending.
findings.detail: The council has implemented "a wider Spending Management Panel to authorise all expenditure over £500" as a financial control measure. This exceptionally low threshold indicates spending discipline at departmental level is considered insufficient and all discretionary spend requires central approval.
findings.matters: A £500 approval threshold signals the council views its financial position as requiring exceptional control measures; it suggests either tight cash flow management, loss of financial discipline at departmental level, or both.
findings.figures: Spending Management Panel approval threshold: £500
findings.quote: The introduction of a wider Spending Management Panel to authorise all expenditure over £500.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 Budget Preparation Process 2026-2027 - Savings Proposals for Consultation Phase 2 - Final
findings.headline: Adult social care, children's placements and temporary accommodation pressures remain unresolved with further reviews still underway.
findings.detail: The document identifies three demand-led service areas as still requiring work: adult social care services, children's placement provision, and temporary accommodation and homelessness. It states "Further reviews and initiatives are being explored but have yet to conclude," indicating these high-cost areas are not yet part of the savings plan.
findings.matters: These are typically the fastest-growing budget areas in local government; unresolved pressures here suggest the deficit could worsen if demand continues to rise, limiting the council's ability to respond to other shocks.
findings.figures: Three specific demand-led areas identified as requiring further unscheduled work
findings.quote: There will remain a focus on demand led service areas such as (i) adult social care services, (ii) children's placement provision, and (iii) the temporary accommodation and homelessness service. Further reviews and initiatives are being explored but have yet to conclude.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 Budget Preparation Process 2026-2027 - Savings Proposals for Consultation Phase 2 - Final
findings.headline: The council's General Fund reserve is below the risk-assessed level and restoration competes with immediate budget pressures.
findings.detail: The S151 Officer and CIPFA have recommended that the General Fund balance be restored to the risk-assessed level at the earliest opportunity. This commitment indicates the reserve has fallen below prudent minimums and needs rebuilding while the council manages a £32 million deficit.
findings.matters: Reserves below assessed adequacy reduce the council's buffer against unexpected pressures and represent a significant vulnerability; rebuilding reserves while managing this deficit requires either further savings or borrowing.
findings.figures: General Fund balance below risk-assessed level
findings.quote: The commitment to restore the General Fund balance to the risk assessed level at the earliest opportunity, as recommended by the S151 Officer and CIPFA.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 Budget Preparation Process 2026-2027 - Savings Proposals for Consultation Phase 2 - Final
findings.headline: Business rates reset and revaluation in 2026/2027 are anticipated to reduce the council's income in real terms.
findings.detail: The 2026/2027 settlement coincides with a full business rates reset and revaluation expected to reduce resources in real terms. Additionally, the provisional settlement will not be announced until the week of 15 December 2025, leaving the council with "very little time for the Council to make changes to its budget should there be significant changes."
findings.matters: A reduction in business rates compounds the council's budget pressure and reduces flexibility; the tight timeline for responding to the provisional settlement (7 weeks before the February budget deadline) limits mitigation options.
findings.figures: Full business rates reset and revaluation planned for 2026/2027; provisional settlement announced week of 15 December 2025
findings.quote: The 2026/2027 settlement, which will be the first three-year settlement in over a decade, coincides with a full business rates reset and revaluation that are anticipated to reduce the resources available to the authority in real terms. The provisional settlement will be announced week commencing 15 December 2025 which will afford very little time for the Council to make changes to its budget should there be significant changes.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 Budget Preparation Process 2026-2027 - Savings Proposals for Consultation Phase 2 - Final
findings.headline: A CIPFA Resilience Review was commissioned due to risks in the 2025/2026 budget, with recommendations to reset the organisation's financial accountability culture.
findings.detail: The council commissioned the Chartered Institute of Public Finance & Accountancy (CIPFA) to carry out a Resilience Review due to "risks inherent in the 2025/2026 Budget and the continuing demand pressures facing the Council." The report sets out "clear recommendations to deliver improvements across the Council and re-set the culture of the organisation in terms of financial accountability."
findings.matters: An external Resilience Review from a professional accountancy body indicates the council's financial management was sufficiently concerning to warrant specialist intervention; this signals governance and control weaknesses that affect credit risk.
findings.figures: CIPFA Resilience Review commissioned and received
findings.quote: In response to the financial pressures, Executive and Full Council commissioned the Chartered Institute of Public Finance & Accountancy (CIPFA) to carry out a Resilience Review of the Council's financial position, recognising the risks inherent in the 2025/2026 Budget and the continuing demand pressures facing the Council.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 Budget Preparation Process 2026-2027 - Savings Proposals for Consultation Phase 2 - Final
findings.headline: Bedford faces a £32.5 million funding gap for 2026/2027 that will not be closed even after both phases of savings proposals.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy projects a £58.6 million cumulative shortfall to 2029/2030, with £32.5 million in 2026/2027. Phase 1 savings totalling £11.5 million were approved in October 2025, and phase 2 proposals total £8.989 million, leaving a shortfall of approximately £12 million for 2026/2027 alone. The council acknowledges the proposals are insufficient to close the gap.
findings.matters: A lender assessing repayment capacity needs to know whether the council can achieve a balanced budget; a £12 million unresolved gap suggests further service cuts or reserves drawdown are inevitable.
findings.figures: £58.6 million cumulative gap to 2029/2030; £32.5 million in 2026/2027; phase 1 £11.5 million; phase 2 £8,989,000
findings.quote: The current proposals do not meet the full gap identified in the MTFS and it is critical that further work is still undertaken to bring forward a balanced budget in 2026/2027

findings.paper_title: Item 09 Revenue Budget Trends
findings.headline: Aged debt of £14.62 million outstanding over 91 days (73.4% of total) with £9.158 million from adult social care, represents material collection risk
findings.detail: As at 30 September 2025, total outstanding debt was £19.929 million, of which £14.62 million has been outstanding longer than 91 days. Of the aged debt, £9.158 million relates to adult social care, including £4.09 million awaiting probate. The profile indicates either collection difficulties or unenforceable debts. The council has established an Adult Services Debt Management Panel and engaged CIPFA to review processes, suggesting recent recognition of weakness.
findings.matters: Large aged debt balances indicate cash flow weakness and reduced actual revenue collection. Probate debt is particularly difficult to recover. This suggests the council's actual revenue position is weaker than the stated forecast.
findings.figures: £14.62 million debt over 91 days (73.4% of £19.929 million total); £9.158 million from adult social care; £4.09 million awaiting probate
findings.quote: The profile of debt highlights that £14.62 million of the debt has been outstanding for longer than 91 days (73.4%) and, as such, represents a risk of non-recovery.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 Revenue Budget Trends
findings.headline: Strategic sourcing savings of £1.500 million included in the budget are not being achieved
findings.detail: The Financing directorate forecast overspend includes £1.500 million due to "shortfall in the anticipated achievement of the strategic sourcing savings". This suggests planned procurement efficiencies are not materialising, indicating either weak budget planning or inability to execute the procurement strategy.
findings.matters: Unachievable efficiency targets suggest the council's budget assumptions are optimistic or execution is poor. This reduces confidence in the council's ability to deliver further savings to close the £11.7m gap.
findings.figures: £1.500 million shortfall in strategic sourcing savings
findings.quote: £1.500 million overspend due to a shortfall in the anticipated achievement of the strategic sourcing savings.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 Revenue Budget Trends
findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy loss of £2.033 million where DWP subsidy covers only 56% of actual costs for Supported Exempt Accommodation
findings.detail: The Resources directorate overspends by £1.652 million, driven by £2.033 million Housing Benefit subsidy shortfall. Supported Exempt Accommodation claims have risen from 386 in April 2025 to 442 by September, with average weekly cost per claim up 10%. The Rent Officer Decision sets subsidy at significantly below rent payable, creating a 44% loss on these claims. SEA claims have grown from 337 in July 2024 to 442 by September. Additional pressure from nightly lets in Temporary Accommodation where subsidy remains at 2011 Local Housing Authority rates despite increased actual costs.
findings.matters: This represents an unfunded welfare obligation growing at 29% per quarter. The council has no control over either subsidy rates or client numbers. If SEA demand continues to accelerate, this loss will deepen.
findings.figures: £2.033 million HB subsidy shortfall; SEA claims 442 (vs 386 in April, 337 in July 2024); 44% loss on SEA subsidy; nightly let subsidy frozen at 2011 rates
findings.quote: The amount of Housing Benefit Subsidy that can be claimed from the DWP for these claims is set by the Rent Officer Decision (independent of the Council) and is significantly below rent payable, therefore, there is a loss on the subsidy received of around 44%.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 Revenue Budget Trends
findings.headline: Adult social care external packages up £2.885 million despite flat client numbers, driven by inflation and increasing case complexity
findings.detail: Adult Services forecast £1.984 million overspend. The primary driver is £2.885 million overspend on external care packages with client numbers similar to 2024/2025. The council attributes this to "inflationary pressures along with clients presenting with greater complexity and increasing needs". There has been a rise in demand for supported living for adults aged 18-64 with mental health needs, learning disabilities and neurodiversity.
findings.matters: Cost escalation on flat caseloads suggests either genuine increase in complexity or failure to secure value for money. This trend is likely to continue and may not be controllable by the council.
findings.figures: Adult Services overspend £1.984 million; external packages overspend £2.885 million; in-house homes overspend £0.527 million (partially offset by staffing underspend)
findings.quote: The forecast variance within Adult Services primarily relates to external care package costs with a net forecast overspend of £2.885 million across all external packages. This is dues to inflationary pressures along with clients presenting with greater complexity and increasing needs.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 Revenue Budget Trends
findings.headline: Children's services overspend of £7.752 million with looked-after children placement costs up 22.2% driven by growing complexity and caseloads
findings.detail: Looked After Children placements are forecast to overspend by £6.380 million. The number of children in care has increased in 2025/2026 compared to 2024/2025, with growth particularly in residential and unregistered placements. Average weekly placement costs have risen above budget. Employee costs add £1.075 million overspend due to agency staff covering vacant Social Worker posts. The Integrated Care Board is not funding complex needs placements, leaving all costs with the council, and "resolving the funding contributions for care placements with the ICB remains in dispute".
findings.matters: This is a rapidly escalating demand pressure with limited control mechanisms. If more children enter care or complexity increases further, costs will spike. The dispute with the ICB over funding obligations is unresolved.
findings.figures: LAC Placements overspend £6.380 million; employee costs overspend £1.075 million; LAC line 22.2% over budget (£8.091m variance on £36.515m budget)
findings.quote: There is currently a forecast overspend on Looked After Children Placements of £6.380 million. This is primarily due to the growth in the number of residential and unregistered placements along with an increase to the average weekly placement cost above that budgeted.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 Revenue Budget Trends
findings.headline: Council forecasts £11.708 million overspend and is preparing to request Exceptional Financial Support from government
findings.detail: As at 30 September 2025, the council forecasts a revenue outturn overspend of £11.708 million against the approved budget. The council acknowledges that "it is highly likely that the budget will not be balanced by the end of the financial year". Officers are engaged with MHCLG regarding a potential application for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), with applications to be considered alongside 2026/2027 applications in February 2026.
findings.matters: A local authority requiring government bailout funding is a material credit event. EFS applications are rare and indicate severe financial distress requiring restructuring.
findings.figures: £11.708 million forecast overspend; General Fund Balance £9.6 million (below recommended limit); £0.5 million in-year contingency
findings.quote: Whilst the financial position has improved it is still a long way from a balanced budget. Officer discussions with MHCLG continue to take place in case, as a last resort, there is a need to make an application to Government for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS).

findings.paper_title: Item 12.4 MTFS
findings.headline: Capital investment programme challenged to prioritise schemes and substantially reduce external borrowing demand, including surplus asset disposals
findings.detail: The capital investment programme has been challenged to prioritise schemes and substantially reduce external borrowing demand. The council is also committing to dispose of surplus assets. This suggests capital projects are being deferred or cancelled to reduce debt service costs.
findings.matters: Deferral of capital investment can mask near-term budget problems but creates longer-term infrastructure decay risk. Asset disposals, if accelerated, may realise lower values in a constrained market.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided in this section
findings.quote: The capital investment programme has been challenged to prioritise capital schemes and substantially reduce the demand for external borrowing. This includes the commitment to dispose of identified surplus assets.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.4 MTFS
findings.headline: Fair Funding 2.0 creates material uncertainty; consultation did not provide provisional allocations at council level
findings.detail: A major government funding reform is underway (Fair Funding 2.0), with provisional allocations to be announced at a later date. The consultation document does not include provisional funding allocations for individual councils, creating significant risk to the accuracy of the MTFS projections. The council's relative needs assessment shows a 9.4% increase compared to the 2013/14 baseline, but actual settlement is not yet known.
findings.matters: The MTFS projections assume certain funding outcomes that may not materialise. If the council's settlement is lower than assumed, the deficit would be larger than forecast. This is a material planning risk.
findings.figures: Bedford's weighted relative need increased 9.4%; unitary average increased only 2.2%; no provisional allocations published
findings.quote: The consultation does not include provisional allocations at local authority level; this has led to widespread criticism to the completeness and transparency of the process. The lack of detail within the consultation provides significant risk to the accuracy of the short, medium and long-term financial planning estimates adopted by the authority.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.4 MTFS
findings.headline: Improvement Plan will not be in place until January 2026, leaving a three-month gap before 2026/27 budget must be set
findings.detail: The Executive has committed to developing a comprehensive Improvement Plan by January 2026, which will set out how the financial challenge will be addressed. However, this Improvement Plan does not yet exist. The council must set a balanced budget for 2026/27 by the statutory deadline, but the detailed roadmap for achieving this will not be complete until one month before final approval.
findings.matters: A three-month window between plan completion and budget approval is tight. If the plan reveals that savings targets are unachievable, there will be little time to secure alternative funding or seek additional government support.
findings.figures: Improvement Plan due: January 2026; Budget setting deadline: late February/early March 2026
findings.quote: The Executive are fully cognisant of the considerable financial challenge and are committed to developing an overarching Improvement Plan by January 2026. This will combine the existing Stability Plan, Resilience Review and other workplans into one document that will set out how the financial challenge over the medium term will be addressed.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.4 MTFS
findings.headline: SEND deficit is £0.327m and covered by a statutory override; override ends 2027/28, creating unknown liability risk
findings.detail: The council currently holds a Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit of £0.327 million. This is covered by a statutory override that allows the deficit to be excluded from the balanced budget requirement. However, this override is due to end on 31 March 2028. The NAO estimates the total SEND deficit across all councils could reach £4.6 billion by March 2026, and without the override extension, 43% of councils would have issued Section 114 notices.
findings.matters: When the statutory override ends, Bedford will be forced to bring the DSG deficit into its revenue budget. The size of the future deficit is unknown but the sector-wide pattern suggests it could be material.
findings.figures: Current DSG deficit: £0.327 million; sector total SEND deficit estimated at £4.6 billion by March 2026; statutory override extended to 2027/28
findings.quote: The total SEND deficit covered by this override is projected to reach £4.6 billion by March 2026. In June 2025, the override was extended to 2027/2028. The NAO estimated in October 2024 that, without this extension, 43 per cent of local authorities would have been at risk of issuing a Section 114 report.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.4 MTFS
findings.headline: Adult and children's social care demand is accelerating; statutory obligations mean costs cannot be capped
findings.detail: Adult social care shows demand growth of 4% per annum, with increasing complexity in cases including young people transitioning from children's services, neuro-diverse needs, and working-age mental health support. Children's services demand is also growing, driven by increasing complexity of placements, SEND costs, and statutory home-to-school transport obligations. Both are ringfenced statutory duties; the council cannot refuse to meet identified need.
findings.matters: Demand-driven statutory spending creates an open-ended liability. If 4% growth assumptions are exceeded, the council must either cut elsewhere or increase borrowing. These are the largest pressure areas in the forecast.
findings.figures: Adult care: 4% annual growth in packages; Children's services: 5% in-house fostering growth, 4% independent placements, 7% direct payments, 2% home-to-school transport
findings.quote: The MTFS reflects the continued trend in growth and demand for adult social care with Adult Services continuing to see higher demand, increasing complexity of need requiring specialist and increased levels of care provision, as well as higher costs in the care market. In particular there is increased demand from; The number and complexity of young people with learning disabilities reaching the age of transition to adult social care (from support provided by Children's Services) People with increasing neuro-diverse needs and Rising levels of people of working age with mental health care or support needs

findings.paper_title: Item 12.4 MTFS
findings.headline: Council is seeking Exceptional Financial Support from government; budget gap would increase by £14.2m if refused
findings.detail: The council is in active discussions with MHCLG seeking Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to bridge the 2026/27 gap. The document reveals that if EFS is refused, the council's budget deficit would increase by £14.2 million in that year alone, forcing either additional service cuts or further reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: Reliance on discretionary central government support that is not guaranteed means the council's financial position is contingent on a political decision outside its control. Refusal would force emergency action mid-budget year.
findings.figures: EFS requested to cover part of £32.5 million gap; refusal would add £14.2 million to deficit
findings.quote: Setting a balanced budget for 2026/2027 alone with a Budget Gap of £32.5 million will need Government Support. The Council is in ongoing discussions with MHCLG regarding the financial position. Should the Council be refused EFS by the Government then the budget gap would increase by the equivalent amount of the overspend (£14.2 million as at July 2025).

findings.paper_title: Item 12.4 MTFS
findings.headline: General Fund balance is below the risk-assessed minimum and has been declining
findings.detail: The General Fund balance stands at £9.6 million, down from £11.2 million as at 31 March 2024. The council's own risk assessment determines the appropriate range to be £13.2-£16.2 million. This shortfall of £3.6-6.6 million means the council is underfunded relative to the financial risks it faces, including demographic and inflationary exposure.
findings.matters: A council falling below its own minimum reserves buffer is drawing down a financial shock-absorber and signalling that it is operating at the edge of prudence. Further erosion could trigger Section 114 notices or force emergency funding requests.
findings.figures: Current balance: £9.6 million; 31 March 2024 balance: £11.2 million; risk-assessed range: £13.2-£16.2 million; current shortfall: £3.6-6.6 million
findings.quote: The General Fund balance is currently at £9.6 million; this is a reduction from the balance of £11.2 million as at 31 March 2024 following drawdown to balance the 2024/2025 outturn. However, given the Council's exposure to demographic and inflationary risk and the uncertain financial landscape, the range of financial risk is assessed as being between £13.2 million and £16.2 million.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.4 MTFS
findings.headline: Business rates reset in 2026/27 will reduce annual income by over £10 million
findings.detail: A full business rates reset is scheduled for 1 April 2026, the first since 2013. Because Bedford has benefited from healthy business growth since 2013, its current business rates yield is significantly above its Baseline Need. The reset will return growth accumulated over 13 years to the government, with the council experiencing an estimated annual reduction exceeding £10 million once transitional arrangements end in 2028/29.
findings.matters: This is a permanent, structural reduction in a key revenue stream that will force further service cuts or borrowing. It is not an assumption risk but a confirmed government policy.
findings.figures: Annual reduction exceeding £10 million; phased over 2026/27 (two-thirds of loss) and 2027/28 (one-third of loss), with full impact from 2028/29
findings.quote: Due to healthy business growth since the establishment of the Business Rates Retention System, Bedford Borough's current business rates yield is significantly above its Baseline Need, on this basis, a reset will detrimentally impact upon its future net resources income; this annual reduction is initially estimated to exceed £10 million.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.4 MTFS
findings.headline: Cumulative deficit of £58.6 million over the medium term with no current savings plan in place
findings.detail: The council faces a cumulative funding gap of £58.6 million for 2026/27 to 2029/30, with £32.5 million in 2026/27 alone. Critically, the MTFS document does not currently incorporate solutions to close this gap; instead, the council is still drawing up an Improvement Plan.
findings.matters: A council unable to explain how it will eliminate a £32.5m annual deficit in the next financial year presents acute refinancing risk. The absence of a detailed plan means the severity and timing of spending cuts are unknown.
findings.figures: £58.6 million cumulative gap (2026/27-2029/30); £32.5 million gap in 2026/27 alone; £12.8 million in 2027/28; £7.9 million in 2028/29; £5.4 million in 2029/30
findings.quote: The MTFS sets out the financial challenge the Council is facing, it does not currently incorporate potential solutions to close the financial shortfall. The Council is drawing up an Improvement Plan that will look to identify options to close the budget gap.

news_drafts.headline: Bedford's 2026/27 budget rests on £25m of government Exceptional Financial Support, and spending is within it
news_drafts.lead:
Bedford Borough Council's 2026/27 budget depends on £25 million of exceptional financial support (EFS), government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending, which is a last resort. The council's papers for the Executive on 14 October say that without it, the council's chief finance officer would have had to issue a section 114 notice, a formal warning that the council cannot balance its budget, which freezes new spending until councillors agree a plan.

The budget was approved on 18 February 2026. The papers state that it "is supported by £25 million Exceptional Financial Support (alongside 36 other councils) without which it would be necessary to issue a s114 notice." Bedford is therefore one of 37 councils given such support for the year.

The latest budget monitoring, the in-year check of spending against budget, covers August. It shows the council within its budget for 2026/27. The papers add that this requires tight financial control to be maintained through to the end of the year. The figures appear in the covering report for the medium-term financial strategy, the council's plan for the next three to five years, which is on the Executive's agenda as item 13.

news_drafts.headline: Bedford ended 2025/26 £17.7m over budget, with £20m of exceptional government support drawn
news_drafts.lead:
Bedford Council finished 2025/26 with a day-to-day spending overspend of £17.726m, about 10% of its £177.616m budget, according to the outturn report (the actual figures once the year has ended) before Full Council on 7 October. The report puts it down mainly to demand in children's and adult social care. The council drew £20m of exceptional financial support (EFS, government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending, a last resort), approved in principle on 23 February 2026, and carried £4.078m forward to strengthen reserves.

The Audit Committee's annual report names children's external placements as a main driver. It says the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government gave £22m of support for 2025/26 and £58m to enable a balanced 2026/27 budget. The latest monitoring report forecasts a 2026/27 overspend of £3.647m as at 30 June 2026, including proposed use of all £25m of EFS approved for the year. Final approval depends on the council's external audit (an independent check of its accounts) being completed at year-end. Mitigation plans had not yet shown an effect by June.

The council's working assumptions show deficits of £32.1m in 2027/28, then £8.0m, £3.9m and £4.4m, reaching £48.4m cumulatively by 2030/31. They assume no EFS beyond 2027/28. In June 2026 the Executive approved a budget strategy committing the council to no more than £10m of EFS beyond 2027/28, aiming to end reliance on it. Directorate savings targets are set and preparation of the 2027/28 budget has been brought forward.

news_drafts.headline: Bedford used £20m of government exceptional support after 2025/26 day-to-day spending ran £17.7m over budget
news_drafts.lead:
Bedford Council used £20m of exceptional financial support (EFS, government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending, a last resort) to balance its 2025/26 revenue budget, its budget and corporate services scrutiny committee was told. Day-to-day spending (revenue spending) overspent by £17.726m against a net budget of £177.616m, equivalent to 10%.

The council's outturn report (the actual figures once the year had ended) puts the overspend down to continuing demand in social care placements, adult care packages and housing support. Operational spending reached £200.261m against a budget of £183.271m. Monthly budget monitoring (the in-year check of spending against budget) ran throughout the year, alongside a Spending Management Panel, a recruitment freeze and a reduction in agency staff. The report says these did not prevent the overspend.

The council applied in December 2025 for up to £22m of support, to cover the forecast deficit and the costs of the Cleat Hill explosion. It was notified on 23 February 2026 that the application was accepted in principle. Of the total, £20m went to the revenue budget and £1.806m to Cleat Hill, leaving £4.078m unused. The council says its discussions with central government on its financial pressures began in January 2025 and continued through the year.
news_drafts.paper_title: Item 08 General Fund Budget and Capital Budget Outturn
